metadata.title: EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health
metadata.summary: The excerpt addresses the classification, diagnosis and management of adult male hypogonadism, with particular attention to late onset hypogonadism. It covers testosterone therapy and other treatment options, contraindications, safety and follow-up. Its methodology also identifies erectile dysfunction and male infertility as sections of the broader guidelines.

conditions_covered: Compensated or subclinical form of hypogonadism
target_population: Adult men with symptoms of hypogonadism
Men with secondary hypogonadism who desire fertility
Men previously treated for prostate cancer
Men with pre-existing cardiovascular disease or elevated haematocrit risk
therapeutic_areas: Conventional medical therapies for severe depressive symptoms and osteoporosis

recognition: An increase above the normal haematocrit range generally appears between three and twelve months after starting testosterone therapy; it can also follow a dose increase, a switch from topical to parenteral treatment, or the development of a relevant comorbidity.

An elevated haematocrit is more likely when the pretreatment value is near the upper limit of normal, particularly with smoking or respiratory disease. Parenteral formulations are associated with higher haematocrit more often than topical formulations.
A registry comparison associated long-acting testosterone undecanoate with a greater risk of haematocrit > 50% than testosterone gels.

In a database study of men receiving testosterone therapy, those who developed haematocrit > 52% had a higher risk of MACE or venous thromboembolism, chiefly during the first year. The risk was greater at a 54% threshold; no increased risk was observed at a 50% threshold.

management.severity: Elevated haematocrit without comorbidity or acute CV or venous thromboembolism
management.actions: Reduce the testosterone dose or change its formulation. For a very high value, consider venesection (500 mL), repeated if necessary; stopping testosterone therapy is usually unnecessary in this situation.
Adjust or withdraw testosterone therapy and perform venesection if required. Once haematocrit has normalised, reintroduce treatment at a lower dose and consider a topical preparation.

prevention: Assess baseline haematocrit before testosterone therapy. Carefully evaluate baseline haematocrit of 48-50%, especially in men with COPD, Obstructive Sleep Apnoea Syndrome (OSAS), or residence at high altitude.
Measure haematocrit at three, six and twelve months after treatment begins and annually thereafter.
Evaluate patients with polycythaemia vera or increased risk of elevated haematocrit every three months during the first year and at least every six months subsequently.
In men with pre-existing CVD who require testosterone therapy, use careful clinical follow-up and regular haematocrit and testosterone measurements; haematocrit should not exceed 54%.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Haematocrit > 54% requires adjustment or withdrawal of testosterone therapy, with venesection if needed. Treatment may be restarted at a lower dose after normalisation, with consideration of a topical formulation.

toxicities.incidence: In the TRAVERSE study, pulmonary embolism occurred in 0.9% of the testosterone therapy group versus 0.5% of the placebo group.
recognition: A family history of venous thromboembolism warrants investigation for an unrecognised thrombophilia-hypofibrinolysis disorder.
One study reported venous thromboembolism in 42 cases, of which 40 had an underlying thrombophilia diagnosis.
The TRAVERSE pulmonary embolism finding requires confirmation; other studies and reviews did not establish an increased venous thromboembolism risk with testosterone therapy.
Patients receiving SERMs should be informed of a possible increased venous thromboembolism risk, although supporting data are lacking.

management.actions: Adjust or withdraw testosterone therapy and use venesection when required to avert potential adverse outcomes, including venous thromboembolism.

prevention: Ask about a family history of venous thromboembolism before initiating testosterone therapy; investigate a positive history and counsel the patient.
Treat men with pre-existing venous-thromboembolism who require testosterone therapy cautiously, with close clinical follow-up and regular haematocrit and testosterone measurements.
Warn patients considering SERMs about the potential venous thromboembolism risk while explaining that data are lacking.
toxicities.dose_modifications: If haematocrit exceeds 54%, adjust or withdraw testosterone therapy. After normalisation, treatment may be resumed at a lower dose, with consideration of a topical preparation.

recognition: In TRAVERSE, testosterone therapy was noninferior to placebo for MACE, while atrial fibrillation occurred somewhat more often in the testosterone group; this observation needs confirmation.
Interventional evidence suggests no increased cardiovascular risk for up to three years of testosterone therapy. Studies beyond that period cannot exclude later cardiovascular events.
In the Framingham Heart Study, HCT > 48% was associated with increased CAD and mortality risk; this was not established specifically for testosterone-induced erythrocytosis.

management.severity: Pre-existing CVD or elevated CVD risk in a man requiring testosterone therapy
management.actions: Use caution, assess cardiovascular symptoms and risk factors, provide close clinical follow-up, and regularly measure testosterone and haematocrit. Refer to a cardiologist for risk stratification and comorbidity treatment when appropriate.

prevention: Assess cardiovascular risk factors before testosterone therapy.
Before treatment, assess cardiovascular symptoms in men with known CVD and continue close clinical evaluation during therapy.

Assess and address individual risk factors, including lifestyle, diet, exercise, smoking, hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia, in men with pre-existing CVD and those receiving androgen deprivation therapy.
toxicities.dose_modifications: If haematocrit exceeds 54% during testosterone therapy, adjust or withdraw treatment; after normalisation, consider restarting at a lower dose or switching to a topical preparation.

recognition: TRAVERSE observed a mildly higher incidence of acute kidney injury in the testosterone group than in the placebo group; confirmation is needed.

toxicities.event: Fluid retention and worsening chronic cardiac failure
recognition: Fluid retention can exacerbate severe chronic cardiac failure.

management.severity: Chronic cardiac failure when testosterone therapy is nevertheless chosen
management.actions: Follow the patient closely through clinical assessments and regular testosterone and haematocrit measurements.

prevention: Avoid testosterone therapy in severe chronic cardiac failure; uncontrolled or poorly controlled congestive heart failure is also listed among its absolute contraindications.

recognition: Exogenous testosterone suppresses pituitary gonadotropin secretion, impairing spermatogenesis and sperm maturation.

management.severity: Hypogonadism in a man seeking fertility
management.actions: Do not use testosterone therapy. For secondary hypogonadism, consider gonadotropin therapy to maintain testosterone levels and restore sperm production.

prevention: Discuss fertility before treatment and avoid testosterone therapy in men who currently wish to have children.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Testosterone therapy is contraindicated when fertility is desired.

toxicities.event: Prostate-specific antigen changes and prostate cancer safety concerns
recognition: TRAVERSE found a significantly greater rise from baseline in total PSA with testosterone therapy than with placebo, without a difference in PCa incidence or high-grade PCa rate between groups at a mean follow-up of 33.0 ± (SD) 12.1 months.
Available evidence does not establish an increased PCa risk from testosterone therapy, but long-term prospective safety data are insufficient, particularly for PCa survivors.
A digital rectal examination can detect prostate abnormalities despite a normal PSA value.

management.severity: Previous surgically treated localised PCa without evidence of active disease
management.actions: Discuss the insufficient long-term safety evidence fully with the patient. Restrict consideration of testosterone therapy to men at low risk of recurrence, after at least one year follow-up with PSA < 0.01 ng/mL.

management.severity: Increase in PSA or detection of a prostate abnormality during treatment
management.actions: Use local PCa guidelines to decide whether to stop testosterone therapy or perform a prostate biopsy.

prevention: Assess PSA and perform a digital rectal examination before testosterone therapy; monitor for prostate abnormalities during treatment.
In PCa survivors receiving testosterone therapy, measure total PSA at three, six and twelve months in the first year and annually thereafter.
Discuss PSA and digital rectal examination screening during testosterone therapy with men aged < 40 or > 70 years.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Whether to discontinue testosterone therapy because of a PSA increase or prostate abnormality should be determined according to local PCa guidelines.

recognition: The document states that testosterone and/or its conversion to E2 can significantly influence breast cancer growth.
Safety information on testosterone therapy after successful treatment of male breast cancer is unavailable.

management.severity: Active or previously treated male breast cancer
management.actions: Do not administer testosterone therapy; counsel previously treated patients that its safety in this setting is unknown.

prevention: Recognise active and previously treated male breast cancer as contraindications to testosterone therapy.

recognition: Studies and meta-analyses did not find a significant worsening of LUTS with testosterone therapy, and some reported limited improvement.
Long-term safety evidence is limited for severe LUTS with IPSS > 19 because such patients have generally been excluded from RCTs.

management.actions: Treat this as a relative contraindication when considering testosterone therapy because long-term safety data are insufficient.

recognition: A mild blood-pressure increase has been reported with the newer oral TU formulations, for which the FDA required a boxed warning.
prevention: Inform candidates for testosterone therapy about formulation-specific risks and benefits; the treatment-monitoring schedule includes blood-pressure measurements.

recognition: Gastrointestinal adverse effects are listed as a disadvantage of this oral formulation.

toxicities.event: Skin irritation and inadvertent transfer during close contact
recognition: Skin irritation is listed for testosterone patches.
Topical testosterone and Dihydrotestosterone gels can transfer during close skin contact; local skin effects are less prominent with gels than with traditional patches.
Gel contamination of the skin at a blood-collection site can produce a falsely elevated testosterone result.
prevention: To reduce transfer from testosterone gel, cover the application site with clothing or apply it to skin that is not ordinarily touched during close contact, such as the inner thigh.
Consider possible contamination of the blood-collection site when interpreting testosterone measurements after gel application; a repeat measurement may be indicated.

recognition: Injection-site pain is listed for Testosterone undecanoate in castor oil.

Older short-acting injectable formulations can cause broad fluctuations in circulating testosterone, which patients may find unpleasant and which may contribute to adverse effects such as polycythaemia.
The buccal system can cause transient gum oedema, blistering, gingivitis, oral irritation or an unpleasant taste.
Nasal irritation is listed for Testosterone nasal.
Implant placement is invasive and carries risks of extrusion and infection at the insertion site.

toxicities.event: Reduced bone density and osteoporosis during anti-oestrogen treatment
recognition: Long-term use of these agents can reduce bone density and lead to osteoporosis, potentially increasing fracture risk.
prevention: Explain potential adverse effects when discussing these off-label treatment options.

recognition: The document finds no evidence that testosterone therapy causes or worsens sleep apnoea.
In one RCT involving severe sleep apnoea, oxygen saturation index and nocturnal hypoxaemia were reduced relative to placebo after seven weeks, but the difference was absent after eighteen weeks.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Check contraindications before testosterone therapy, including locally advanced or metastatic PCa, male breast cancer, an active wish to have children, haematocrit ≥ 54%, and uncontrolled or poorly controlled congestive heart failure.
Assess cardiovascular risk factors and enquire about a family history of venous thromboembolism before starting testosterone therapy.

Monitor haematocrit and testosterone at three, six and twelve months after starting testosterone therapy and annually thereafter; increase the frequency of haematocrit assessment for patients at higher risk of erythrocytosis.
prophylaxis.target_population: Men receiving testosterone therapy; more frequent assessment applies to those with polycythaemia vera or increased erythrocytosis risk
prophylaxis.duration: Every three months during the first year and at least every six months thereafter for higher-risk patients

prophylaxis.recommendation: Measure total PSA at three, six and twelve months during the first year of testosterone therapy and annually thereafter.
prophylaxis.duration: During the first year and annually thereafter

infection_management.management: Follow men who have recovered from COVID-19 to exclude long-term effects on sperm and testosterone production. The role of testosterone therapy during acute COVID-19 is unknown.

therapies_index.name: testosterone therapy
therapies_index.mechanism: Exogenous testosterone raises circulating testosterone but suppresses pituitary gonadotropin secretion and spermatogenesis.
approved_indications: Symptomatic hypogonadism with total testosterone < 12 nmol/L when specific contraindications are absent.
First-line treatment for mild erectile dysfunction in men with hypogonadism.
key_toxicities: Elevated haematocrit and polycythaemia.
Suppressed sperm production and maturation.
Fluid retention that can aggravate severe chronic cardiac failure.
monitoring: Assess symptoms after three months; arrange later assessments at six months or twelve months according to clinical and biochemical findings.
Measure testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months after initiation, then annually.
Assess PSA and perform digital rectal examination before treatment and during follow-up.
For patients at high risk of elevated haematocrit, assess every three months during the first year and at least every six months thereafter.
If haematocrit exceeds 54%, adjust or stop treatment and consider venesection; treatment may be restarted at a lower dose after haematocrit normalises.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone undecanoate
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Oral: 120-240 mg 2 or 3 times daily, taken with meals.
key_toxicities: Absorption varies with dietary fat content.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone undecanoate self-emulsifying delivery system
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Oral: 100-237 mg 2 times daily.
key_toxicities: Gastrointestinal adverse effects.
Increased blood pressure.

therapies_index.name: TU caps
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Oral formulation; its absorption is strongly affected by the fat content of food.
key_toxicities: Poor and diet-dependent bioavailability.

therapies_index.name: Mesterolone
therapies_index.mechanism: A 5α-DHT derivative that cannot be converted to oestrogens.
approved_indications: Limited-duration use for particular indications, including painful gynaecomastia.
therapies_index.administration: Oral: 50-100 mg 2 or 3 times daily.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone enanthate
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Injection: 250 mg every 2-3 weeks.
key_toxicities: Fluctuating circulating testosterone concentrations.
Relative risk of polycythaemia.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone cypionate
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Injection: 200 mg every 2-3 weeks.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone propionate
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: The formulation table lists 100 mg every 2 days; the accompanying discussion describes fractionated doses, usually 50 mg, every two to three days.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone ester mixture
therapies_index.mechanism: The mixed esters provide sustained testosterone release into the circulation.
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Injection: 250 mg every 3 weeks. Its stated composition is propionate (30mg), phenylpropionate (60mg), isocaproate (60mg), decanoate (100mg).

therapies_index.name: Testosterone undecanoate in castor oil
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Long-acting injection: the formulation table lists 1,000 mg every 10-14 weeks or 750 mg every 10 weeks. The discussion describes 1,000 mg initially every twelve weeks after a six-week loading dose, with adjustment to ten to fourteen weeks according to the level before injection after three to five injections.
key_toxicities: Injection-site pain.
Adverse effects cannot be addressed by rapid withdrawal because the preparation is long-acting.
monitoring: Check the pre-injection testosterone level to adjust the interval; the therapeutic range described is usually > 12 and < 18 nmol/L.

therapies_index.name: Surgical implants
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Implantation of 4-6 200 mg testosterone implants lasting up to 6 months; the discussion describes testosterone pellets lasting from four to seven months.
key_toxicities: Invasive placement.
Implant extrusion.
Infection at the placement site.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone patches
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Transdermal: 50-100 mg/ day.
key_toxicities: Skin irritation.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone gel 1-2%
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism; gels are suggested instead of long-acting depot preparations when initiating treatment in high-risk men.
therapies_index.administration: Transdermal: 50-100 mg/ day.
key_toxicities: Transfer to another person through close skin contact.
Possible local skin adverse effects.
monitoring: Collect blood two to four hours after gel application when assessing the absorbed testosterone peak; a repeat measurement may be needed if contamination of the sampling site is suspected.

therapies_index.name: Underarm testosterone (testosterone solution 2%)
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Apply 60-120 mg/ day to the underarm with a metered-dose applicator.
monitoring: Monitor testosterone levels to adjust the dose.

therapies_index.name: Dihydrotestosterone gel 2.5%
therapies_index.mechanism: DHT cannot be aromatised to oestrogens.
approved_indications: Use for particular conditions, including gynaecomastia and microphallus.
therapies_index.administration: Transdermal: 34-70 mg/day.
key_toxicities: Transfer to another person through intimate skin contact.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone buccal system
approved_indications: Restoration of testosterone to the physiological range in hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Sustained-release mucoadhesive tablet placed on the upper gums. The discussion describes twice-daily application and removal after 12 hours; the formulation table lists 60 mg 3 times daily.
key_toxicities: Gum oedema.
Blistering.
Gingivitis.
Oral irritation.
Unpleasant taste.

therapies_index.name: Testosterone nasal
approved_indications: Treatment of hypogonadism.
therapies_index.administration: Intranasal gel administered with a metered-dose pump two or three times daily; the formulation table lists 33 mg 3 times daily.
key_toxicities: Nasal irritation.

therapies_index.name: Human chorionic gonadotrophin (HCG)
therapies_index.mechanism: Gonadotropin treatment substitutes deficient stimulation in secondary hypogonadism.
approved_indications: Treatment of secondary hypogonadism in men who desire paternity.
therapies_index.administration: The urine-derived extractive preparation is given at 1,000-2,000 IU 3 times/week.

therapies_index.name: recombinant hCG (rhCG)
therapies_index.mechanism: Gonadotropin treatment substitutes deficient stimulation in secondary hypogonadism.
approved_indications: Treatment of secondary hypogonadism in men who desire paternity.

therapies_index.name: Luteotropic hormone (LH)
therapies_index.mechanism: Gonadotropin treatment substitutes deficient stimulation in secondary hypogonadism.
approved_indications: Treatment of secondary hypogonadism when fertility is desired.

therapies_index.name: recombinant LH (rLH)
therapies_index.mechanism: Gonadotropin treatment substitutes deficient stimulation in secondary hypogonadism.
approved_indications: Treatment of secondary hypogonadism when fertility is desired.

therapies_index.name: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
therapies_index.mechanism: Gonadotropin treatment substitutes deficient stimulation in secondary hypogonadism.
approved_indications: Treatment of secondary hypogonadism in men seeking fertility.
therapies_index.administration: The urine-derived extractive preparation is given at 75-150 IU 3 times/week.

therapies_index.name: recombinant FSH (rFSH)
therapies_index.mechanism: Gonadotropin treatment substitutes deficient stimulation in secondary hypogonadism.
approved_indications: Treatment of secondary hypogonadism in men seeking fertility.
therapies_index.administration: 75-150 IU 3 times/week.

therapies_index.name: hCG with FSH
therapies_index.mechanism: Combined gonadotropin treatment replaces deficient testicular stimulation in secondary hypogonadism.
approved_indications: Restoration of fertility in men with secondary hypogonadism who desire paternity.

therapies_index.name: testosterone and PDE5Is
approved_indications: More severe erectile dysfunction in men with hypogonadism.

therapies_index.name: phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (PDE5Is)
approved_indications: Treatment of erectile dysfunction; concomitant use with testosterone therapy may be needed in men with a comorbidity such as T2DM.

therapies_index.name: selective oestrogen receptor (ER) modulators (SERMs)
therapies_index.mechanism: Bind ERs and act as agonists or antagonists according to the target tissue, helping prevent oestrogen-mediated down-regulation of the HPG axis.
approved_indications: Suggested off-label use to restore testosterone and fertility in functional secondary hypogonadism or idiopathic infertility.
A therapeutic option in male breast cancer.
key_toxicities: Potential predisposition to venous thromboembolism; supporting data are lacking.
Reduced bone density and osteoporosis with long-term use, potentially increasing fracture risk.

therapies_index.name: aromatase inhibitors (AI)
therapies_index.mechanism: Prevent aromatase from converting androgens into oestrogens, thereby countering oestrogen-mediated down-regulation of the HPG axis.
approved_indications: Suggested off-label use to restore testosterone and fertility in functional secondary hypogonadism or idiopathic infertility.
key_toxicities: Reduced bone density and osteoporosis with long-term use, potentially increasing fracture risk.

therapies_index.administration: Lifestyle measures discussed include a low-calorie diet and regular physical activity.
