treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with functional hypogonadism associated with obesity, metabolic disorders, other comorbidities or medicines that impair testosterone production.
decision_rules: Exclude an organic cause before classifying hypogonadism as functional.
Address reversible contributors before considering testosterone therapy: improve lifestyle, reduce excess weight, treat comorbidities and withdraw interfering medicines when possible.

recommended_regimens.name: Weight loss and lifestyle changes
recommended_regimens.summary: Use lifestyle improvement and weight reduction as the initial approach in overweight or obese men with hypogonadism; a low-calorie diet and regular physical activity can raise testosterone modestly.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The reported rise in testosterone after a low-calorie diet and physical activity is small (1-2 nmol). Reported weight regain is 60-86% after three years and 75-121% after five years.

recommended_regimens.name: Treatment of co-morbidities and withdrawal of interfering drugs
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat other contributing conditions and discontinue medicines that impair testosterone production when feasible, before starting testosterone therapy.

not_recommended.name: Testosterone therapy to reduce weight and enhance cardio-metabolic status
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against these uses; evidence for changes in weight and metabolic outcomes is conflicting, and testosterone therapy is intended to address specific hypogonadal symptoms.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The distinction between functional and organic hypogonadism remains debated. Evidence that adding testosterone therapy to lifestyle intervention improves outcomes in symptomatic hypogonadal men is limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Symptomatic men with primary hypogonadism who do not have a contraindication to testosterone therapy.
decision_rules: Treat an identifiable organic cause when indicated.
Testosterone therapy can be considered for symptomatic primary hypogonadism, but it suppresses the HPT axis and can impair fertility.
Discuss the expected benefits and adverse effects of each available preparation and choose a formulation jointly with the patient.

recommended_regimens.name: Testosterone therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Administer exogenous testosterone to restore testosterone levels and improve symptoms when treatment is indicated and contraindications are absent.

not_recommended.name: Testosterone therapy in men who desire fertility
not_recommended.reason: Exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotropin secretion and spermatogenesis.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Unlike secondary hypogonadism, treatment of primary hypogonadism is not described as a way to restore both fertility and testosterone production.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with secondary hypogonadism who desire paternity.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: Low or inappropriately normal gonadotropin levels.
decision_rules: Treat an organic cause, such as a pituitary mass or hyperprolactinemia, when indicated.
When fertility is desired, replace the gonadotropin deficiency rather than prescribe exogenous testosterone.
The guideline reports better outcomes with hCG administered together with FSH than with hCG alone.

recommended_regimens.name: Gonadotropin therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use gonadotropins as the standard treatment to maintain testosterone levels and restore sperm production in men with secondary hypogonadism seeking paternity.

recommended_regimens.name: hCG with FSH
recommended_regimens.summary: Give hCG in combination with FSH; the guideline cites a meta-analysis reporting better outcomes with combined treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Recombinant hCG (rhCG) and LH (rLH) formulations
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline describes effects comparable to urinary-derived preparations.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection among available gonadotropin preparations.

alternative_regimens.name: recombinant FSH (rFSH)
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline describes effects comparable to urinary-derived FSH preparations.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection of the FSH component of gonadotropin therapy.

not_recommended.name: Testosterone therapy in men seeking fertility treatment
not_recommended.reason: It inhibits pituitary gonadotropin secretion, impairing spermatogenesis and sperm maturation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The preparation table lists extractive HCG at 1,000-2,000 IU 3 times/week and extractive or recombinant FSH at 75-150 IU 3 times/week; it gives no dosage data in men for recombinant HCG or recombinant LH.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with persistent specific symptoms of hypogonadism, biochemically confirmed low testosterone and no specific contraindication to treatment.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: Total testosterone < 12 nmol/L; confirm a pathological result on a separate occasion before starting testosterone therapy.
decision_rules: Consider testosterone therapy when symptomatic hypogonadism is confirmed and contraindications have been excluded.
Address treatable organic causes, comorbidities, lifestyle factors and medicines that interfere with testosterone production before initiating therapy when possible.
Explain the benefits and adverse effects of the available preparations and select one through a shared decision.
In high-risk men starting treatment, use testosterone gels rather than long-acting depot administration.

recommended_regimens.name: Testosterone therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use an appropriate testosterone preparation to restore levels and address symptoms in eligible men.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports that meta-analyses found treatment ineffective when baseline testosterone was > 12 nmol/L (3.5 ng/mL), with positive outcomes when levels were < 12 nmol/L and larger effects in symptomatic men with levels < 8 nmol/L.

recommended_regimens.name: Testosterone gels
recommended_regimens.summary: Prefer a gel over a long-acting depot preparation when initiating treatment in high-risk men. The guideline identifies gels and long-acting injectable TU as preparations with optimal safety profiles.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone undecanoate in castor oil
alternative_regimens.summary: A long-acting injectable TU preparation maintains relatively stable testosterone levels. The preparation table lists 1,000 mg every 10-14 weeks and 750 mg every 10 weeks; the narrative describes 1,000 mg initially every twelve weeks after a six-week loading dose, adjustable to every ten to fourteen weeks according to the trough level after three to five injections.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available long-acting option selected according to clinical circumstances and patient preferences; a gel is preferred at initiation in high-risk men.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone undecanoate
alternative_regimens.summary: The oral preparation table lists 120-240 mg 2 or 3 times daily. Absorption depends on dietary fat content, and it must be taken with meals.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available oral preparation chosen according to clinical circumstances and patient preferences.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone undecanoate self-emulsifying delivery system
alternative_regimens.summary: The oral preparation table lists 100-237 mg 2 times daily. The guideline reports gastrointestinal adverse effects and increased blood pressure with this preparation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available oral preparation selected after discussing its benefits and risks.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone enanthate
alternative_regimens.summary: The injectable preparation table lists 250 mg every 2-3 weeks. Older short-acting injectable formulations can cause fluctuations in circulating testosterone and may contribute to polycythaemia.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available injectable option selected according to clinical circumstances and patient preferences.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone cypionate
alternative_regimens.summary: The injectable preparation table lists 200 mg every 2-3 weeks.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available injectable option selected according to clinical circumstances and patient preferences.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone propionate
alternative_regimens.summary: The preparation table lists 100 mg every 2 days; the narrative describes the need for multiple fractionated doses, usually 50 mg every two to three days.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available short-acting injectable option, subject to its frequent-administration limitation.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone ester mixture
alternative_regimens.summary: The preparation table lists 250 mg every 3 weeks. The guideline describes a mixed-ester injectable formulation as available in some countries.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available injectable option where marketed.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone patches
alternative_regimens.summary: The transdermal preparation table lists 50-100 mg/ day and identifies skin irritation and daily administration as disadvantages.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available transdermal option selected according to clinical circumstances and patient preferences.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone gel 1-2%
alternative_regimens.summary: The preparation table lists 50-100 mg/ day. Close skin contact can transfer testosterone to another person.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection of an available gel formulation.

alternative_regimens.name: Underarm testosterone (testosterone solution 2%)
alternative_regimens.summary: The preparation table lists 60-120 mg/ day. The solution is applied under the arm once daily with a metered-dose applicator and is not available in Europe.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An option where the preparation is available.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone buccal system
alternative_regimens.summary: The preparation table lists 60 mg 3 times daily, while the narrative describes twice-daily application to the upper gums and removal after 12 hours.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An option in countries where the buccal system is available; the document gives inconsistent administration frequencies.

alternative_regimens.name: Testosterone nasal
alternative_regimens.summary: The preparation table lists 33 mg 3 times daily; the narrative describes administration two or three times daily and reports preliminary evidence of less Gn suppression and a lower risk of haematocrit increases.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An option in countries where the intranasal gel is available.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical implants
alternative_regimens.summary: The preparation table lists 4-6 200 mg implants lasting up to 6 months. Implantation is invasive.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An option in the limited number of countries where testosterone pellets are available.

not_recommended.name: Testosterone therapy in eugonadal men
not_recommended.reason: The guideline recommends against its use and reports no evidence of benefit for sexual dysfunction in this population.

not_recommended.name: Testosterone therapy in men with an active desire to have children
Testosterone therapy in men with active prostate cancer or breast cancer
not_recommended.reason: These cancers are contraindications to treatment.

response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms and testosterone after treatment initiation.
response_assessment.interpretation: The guideline reports that sexual symptoms may improve by this assessment.

response_assessment.timepoint: three, six and twelve months; annually thereafter
response_assessment.method: Measure testosterone and haematocrit; assess clinical response and safety.
response_assessment.interpretation: A haematocrit > 54% requires adjustment or withdrawal of testosterone therapy and venesection if necessary.

supportive_care: Counsel patients about formulation-specific risks and benefits.
For testosterone gels, reduce transfer through skin contact by covering the application area with clothing or applying gel to skin less likely to be touched.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline gives a relative contraindication for severe LUTS with IPSS score > 19. Baseline haematocrit 48-50% and a family history of venous thromboembolism also require careful evaluation. For gels, blood sampling two to four hours after application can help assess the absorbed peak; contamination of the sampling site can falsely elevate the result.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Hypogonadal men with mild erectile dysfunction (ED).
decision_rules: Use testosterone therapy as the initial treatment for mild ED when hypogonadism is present.
Do not apply this approach to eugonadal men.

recommended_regimens.name: Testosterone therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as first-line treatment for mild ED in hypogonadal men.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited meta-analysis found a greater improvement in erectile function among men with total testosterone < 8 nmol/L than among those with milder hypogonadism, described as total testosterone < 12 nmol/L; testosterone therapy alone produced a clinically effective result only in patients with milder ED.

not_recommended.name: Testosterone therapy for sexual dysfunction in eugonadal men
not_recommended.reason: The guideline reports no evidence of benefit in this population and recommends against testosterone therapy in eugonadal men.

response_assessment.method: Reassess sexual symptoms after starting testosterone therapy.
response_assessment.interpretation: The guideline reports improvement in sexual symptoms as early as this timepoint.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Metabolic comorbidity, including diabetes and obesity, can reduce the magnitude of improvement in erectile function and sexual desire.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Hypogonadal men with more severe erectile dysfunction (ED).
decision_rules: Use combined treatment rather than relying on testosterone therapy alone for more severe ED.

recommended_regimens.name: phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors and testosterone therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use the combination for more severe ED in men with hypogonadism.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited meta-analysis of 913 patients from eight RCTs suggested superior improvement in erectile function with testosterone plus PDE5Is compared with PDE5Is alone; the specific contribution of combined treatment remains unclear.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Men with comorbidity such as T2DM generally experience modest sexual-function improvements with testosterone therapy. The guideline reports insufficient information on combining testosterone therapy with other ED drug therapies.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Hypogonadal men with severe depressive symptoms or a clinical depressive disorder.
decision_rules: Use conventional medical treatment for severe depressive symptoms rather than testosterone therapy as the treatment for depression.

recommended_regimens.name: conventional medical therapies
recommended_regimens.summary: Use established medical treatment for severe depressive symptoms; the guideline does not specify an individual regimen.

not_recommended.name: Testosterone therapy alone for clinical depressive disorders
not_recommended.reason: The guideline reports that findings from TRAVERSE do not support it as an effective treatment option for most men with clinical depressive disorders.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports small improvements in mood and milder depressive symptoms with testosterone therapy, but distinguishes these findings from treatment of severe depression.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Hypogonadal men with osteoporosis or a high risk of bone fracture.
decision_rules: Prioritise antiresorptive treatment when fracture risk is high.
Offer combined antiresorptive treatment and testosterone therapy only when symptoms attributable to hypogonadism are also present.

recommended_regimens.name: antiresorptive therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as the first-choice treatment for hypogonadal men at high risk of bone fracture.

recommended_regimens.name: conventional medical therapies
recommended_regimens.summary: Use conventional medical treatment for osteoporosis; the guideline does not name a specific medicine.

alternative_regimens.name: anti-resorptive treatment and testosterone therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: The combination may be offered when osteoporosis management is accompanied by treatment of hypogonadism-related symptoms.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Hypogonadism-related symptoms are present.

not_recommended.name: Testosterone therapy alone to prevent fractures
not_recommended.reason: Available evidence is insufficient to establish its effect on fracture risk, and its adjunctive role with antiresorptive treatment in high-risk patients has not been established.

response_assessment.method: Consider a DEXA bone scan, particularly in patients with more severe hypogonadism.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports increased BMD with testosterone therapy but states that evidence is insufficient to determine whether testosterone therapy alone reduces fractures.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Hypogonadal men with painful gynaecomastia, or men with particular indications for DHT such as gynaecomastia or microphallus.
decision_rules: Consider these preparations only for the specific indications described, not as unrestricted long-term substitutes for testosterone.

alternative_regimens.name: Mesterolone
alternative_regimens.summary: An oral 5α-DHT derivative that may be used for a limited period for specific indications such as painful gynaecomastia. The preparation table lists 50-100 mg 2 or 3 times daily.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A specific indication such as painful gynaecomastia.

alternative_regimens.name: Dihydrotestosterone gel 2.5%
alternative_regimens.summary: A preparation available in some European countries for particular conditions such as gynaecomastia and microphallus. The preparation table lists 34-70 mg/day.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A particular indication and local availability.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline limits long-term Mesterolone use because it lacks the full spectrum of testosterone bioactivity. Neither Mesterolone nor DHT is aromatised.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with functional secondary hypogonadism or idiopathic infertility, particularly those with obesity or metabolic disorders.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: An intact HPG axis is required.
decision_rules: Anti-oestrogens have been suggested as off-label options to restore testosterone levels and fertility.
Do not expect them to work in primary hypogonadism or secondary hypogonadism caused by organic HPG-axis damage.

alternative_regimens.name: SERMs
alternative_regimens.summary: Off-label agents suggested to restore testosterone levels and fertility; the guideline characterises the supporting evidence as poor.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An intact HPG axis in functional secondary hypogonadism or idiopathic infertility, with counselling about a potential venous thromboembolism risk despite a lack of data.

alternative_regimens.name: AI
alternative_regimens.summary: Off-label agents suggested to restore testosterone levels and fertility; the guideline characterises the supporting evidence as poor.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An intact HPG axis in functional secondary hypogonadism or idiopathic infertility.

not_recommended.name: SERMs and AI in primary hypogonadism or secondary hypogonadism due to organic damage of the HPG axis
not_recommended.reason: Their proposed action requires an intact HPG axis.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Long-term use of these agents may reduce bone density and lead to osteoporosis, potentially increasing fracture risk.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Symptomatic hypogonadal men previously treated surgically for localised prostate cancer (PCa), without evidence of active disease and at low risk of recurrence.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: PSA level < 0.01 ng/mL after at least one year follow-up.
decision_rules: Restrict consideration of testosterone therapy to patients at low risk of recurrent PCa.
Discuss the insufficient long-term safety evidence fully before a treatment decision.
Start treatment only after the specified follow-up and PSA criteria are met.

alternative_regimens.name: testosterone therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered cautiously for symptomatic hypogonadism after surgical treatment of localised PCa.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No evidence of active disease, low recurrence risk, at least one year follow-up and PSA level < 0.01 ng/mL.

not_recommended.name: testosterone therapy in advanced PCa
not_recommended.reason: The guideline states that testosterone administration must be avoided in men with advanced PCa.

response_assessment.timepoint: three, six and twelve months during the first year; annually thereafter
response_assessment.interpretation: Base decisions to stop testosterone therapy or perform prostate biopsy after a PSA increase or prostate abnormality on local PCa guidelines.

supportive_care: Counsel patients that long-term safety with respect to PCa recurrence or progression has not been established.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline rates both counselling about limited long-term safety evidence and restriction to low-recurrence-risk patients as Weak recommendations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Hypogonadal men with pre-existing CVD, previous venous-thromboembolism or chronic cardiac failure who require testosterone therapy.
decision_rules: Assess cardiovascular risk factors before testosterone therapy and assess cardiovascular symptoms in men with known CVD.
Treat patients who require testosterone therapy cautiously, with close clinical follow-up and regular testosterone and haematocrit measurements.
Do not use testosterone therapy solely to improve cardiovascular risk or cardio-metabolic status.
Testosterone therapy is contraindicated in severe chronic cardiac failure because fluid retention may worsen the condition.

alternative_regimens.name: testosterone therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be given for symptomatic hypogonadism with careful monitoring when treatment is required despite pre-existing CVD, venous-thromboembolism or chronic cardiac failure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Clinical assessment supports treatment, severe chronic cardiac failure is absent, and haematocrit is kept from exceeding 54%.

not_recommended.name: testosterone therapy in severe chronic cardiac failure
not_recommended.reason: Fluid retention may exacerbate cardiac failure.

not_recommended.name: testosterone therapy solely for cardiovascular risk reduction
not_recommended.reason: The guideline does not recommend its use outside treatment of specific hypogonadal symptoms on the basis of the equivocal cardiovascular-risk evidence.

response_assessment.method: Perform close clinical assessment and measure testosterone and haematocrit regularly.

supportive_care: Assess and treat individual cardiovascular risk factors, including lifestyle, diet, exercise, smoking, hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia.
Refer to a cardiologist for risk stratification and comorbidity treatment when appropriate.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline rates cautious treatment and monitoring in men with pre-existing CVD, venous-thromboembolism or chronic cardiac failure as Weak. It reports that longer-term cardiovascular safety beyond the studied period remains uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men receiving testosterone therapy who develop elevated haematocrit, including those at increased risk of erythrocytosis.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: Haematocrit > 54% during testosterone therapy; haematocrit 48-50% at baseline warrants careful evaluation before treatment.
decision_rules: If haematocrit exceeds 54%, adjust or withdraw testosterone therapy and perform venesection when required.
Once haematocrit normalises, reintroduce testosterone therapy at a lower dose and consider changing to a topical preparation.
In a patient at lower risk of clinically relevant complications, dose reduction, a change in formulation and venesection may allow testosterone therapy to continue.

recommended_regimens.name: testosterone therapy adjustment or withdrawal
recommended_regimens.summary: Respond to haematocrit > 54% by adjusting or stopping testosterone therapy; use venesection if necessary and consider subsequent reintroduction at a lower dose.

alternative_regimens.name: venesection
alternative_regimens.summary: For a very high haematocrit, the guideline describes removal of 500 mL, repeated if necessary.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Clinically significant elevation, with the decision to interrupt testosterone therapy guided by the clinical situation and risk.

alternative_regimens.name: topical testosterone preparations
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider switching from a parenteral formulation after haematocrit has normalised, alongside a lower dose when testosterone therapy is reintroduced.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Continuation or reintroduction of treatment after testosterone-associated haematocrit elevation.

response_assessment.timepoint: three, six and twelve months after initiation; annually thereafter
every three months during the first year; at least every six months thereafter
response_assessment.method: Evaluate men with polycythaemia vera or a higher risk of elevated haematocrit.

supportive_care: Investigate a family history of venous-thromboembolism before testosterone therapy and counsel affected patients about possible thrombophilia-hypofibrinolysis.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Risk factors for raised haematocrit described by the guideline include a high-normal baseline value, smoking and respiratory conditions. The guideline reports more frequent elevation with parenteral than topical formulations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with active male breast cancer or a history of treatment for male breast cancer who also have hypogonadism.
decision_rules: Recognise active and previously treated male breast cancer as contraindications to testosterone therapy.
Advise previously treated patients that the safety of testosterone therapy in their situation is unknown.

not_recommended.name: testosterone therapy
not_recommended.reason: The guideline treats active and previously treated male breast cancer as absolute contraindications and reports no safety information after successful breast cancer treatment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline mentions SERMs as a treatment option in the management of male breast cancer but does not provide a cancer-treatment regimen in this section.

conditions.name: Male hypogonadism
conditions.description: A clinical syndrome involving symptoms, with or without signs, alongside biochemical testosterone deficiency. It may involve reduced testicular androgen production, impaired sperm production, or both. Its effects can extend to multiple organs and quality of life.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported incidence is between 12.3 and 11.7 cases per 1,000 people per year.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations depend partly on the age at onset. Disease arising in foetal life may cause markedly reduced virilisation, whereas onset before or around puberty may cause delayed puberty and a eunuchoid phenotype. After puberty, particularly with ageing, manifestations may be mild and mistaken for effects of ageing.

subtypes.name: Secondary Hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Inadequate hypothalamic-pituitary stimulation of the testes produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

subtypes.name: Late onset hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Adult-onset disease requires persistent specific symptoms and biochemical testosterone deficiency; its origin may be organic or functional, primary or secondary.

subtypes.name: Functional hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Associated with comorbidities or other influences on the HPG axis, without an identified organic alteration; diagnosis requires exclusion of an organic cause.

subtypes.name: Classical hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Congenital or acquired disease causes structural or irreversible impairment of the pituitary gland, testes, or both.

subtypes.name: compensated or subclinical form of hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Serum testosterone remains normal while LH is elevated; its clinical significance is uncertain.

subtypes.name: ANDROGEN RESISTANCE/DECREASED TESTOSTERONE BIOACTIVITY
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Conditions reduce cellular responsiveness to testosterone or its metabolites.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess compatible symptoms and signs, comorbidities, fertility wishes, potentially interfering drugs and substances, and a history of cryptorchidism or hypospadias surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In patients undergoing evaluation for hypogonadism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Headache or visual disturbance may suggest pituitary disease; a history of cryptorchidism or hypospadias surgery may point to a congenital defect.

diagnostic_workup.test: body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess obesity, which commonly accompanies hypogonadism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In all individuals undergoing assessment.

diagnostic_workup.test: Examination of testicular size, penile size and secondary sexual characteristics
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess androgen status and features of earlier-onset disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During physical evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.test: Upper segment/lower segment ratio and arm-span to height ratio
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a eunuchoid body shape, particularly when disease began before puberty or puberty was delayed.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When an early-onset phenotype is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The stated normal values are > 0.92 for upper segment/lower segment ratio and < 1.0 for arm-span to height ratio.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish biochemical testosterone deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain morning samples between 07.00 and 11.00 hours while fasting; confirm an initial pathological result before testosterone therapy. Avoid measurement during acute disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Persistently low results must be considered alongside compatible symptoms and signs.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate primary from secondary hypogonadism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When pathological total testosterone is detected or the origin of testosterone deficiency needs investigation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated LH accompanies primary hypogonadism; reduced or inappropriately normal gonadotropins accompany secondary hypogonadism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate secondary or potentially organic causes and assess reduced sexual desire.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: With pathological total testosterone; also consider it for reduced sexual desire or other suggestive symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Confirmed hyperprolactinemia warrants pituitary evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible pituitary disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For visual disturbance, headache, confirmed hyperprolactinemia, symptoms of a pituitary mass or another anterior pituitary hormone deficiency. Limited evidence also supports imaging in severe secondary hypogonadism with total testosterone < 6 nmol/L, 1.75 ng/mL and inadequate gonadotropins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected pituitary disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: With suggestive symptoms or confirmed hyperprolactinemia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for prostate abnormalities before testosterone therapy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before any form of testosterone therapy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reduced prostate volume may also support suspicion of hypogonadism.

follow_up.schedule: For patients receiving testosterone therapy, assess treatment at three months, with subsequent assessment at six months or twelve months according to clinical and biochemical findings. Monitor testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months, then annually. Assess patients at high risk of raised haematocrit every three months during the first year and at least every six months thereafter.
recommended_tests: Assess symptoms at baseline, three, six and twelve months, then annually.
Measure testosterone, haematocrit and PSA before and during treatment.
Perform DRE at baseline and at least annually.
Consider a glyco-metabolic profile at baseline and at least annually.
Consider DEXA at baseline and 18-24 months, particularly with more severe hypogonadism.
long_term_effects: Monitor for raised haematocrit, particularly after treatment initiation, dose increases or a change to parenteral treatment.
Assess prostate findings and PSA during treatment.
Monitor cardiovascular status carefully in patients with pre-existing CVD or elevated cardiovascular risk.

conditions.name: Primary Hypogonadism
conditions.description: Hypogonadism arising from impaired testicular function. Listed causes include congenital or developmental disorders, acquired testicular injury or disease, drug exposures and systemic conditions; some systemic conditions can affect both central and peripheral function.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms and signs need not differ from those of secondary hypogonadism. A milder peripheral defect presenting before or around puberty may produce delayed puberty and a eunuchoid phenotype.

subtypes.name: Klinefelter syndrome
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A genetic cause associated with a 47,XXY karyotype.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document testosterone deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When compatible symptoms or signs are present; obtain fasting morning measurements and confirm a pathological result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Interpret together with symptoms, signs and gonadotropin levels.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish testicular from central causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When testosterone deficiency is identified.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated LH supports primary rather than secondary hypogonadism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify possible congenital, acquired, treatment-related or systemic causes and assess fertility wishes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.

follow_up.schedule: When testosterone therapy is used, review at three months and subsequently according to clinical and biochemical findings; monitor testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months, then annually.
recommended_tests: Testosterone
Haematocrit
PSA
Digital rectal examination
long_term_effects: Exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotropin secretion and spermatogenesis.
Monitor for elevated haematocrit and prostate abnormalities during testosterone therapy.

conditions.name: Secondary Hypogonadism
conditions.description: Hypogonadism resulting from insufficient hypothalamic-pituitary stimulation of the testes. Causes described include congenital disorders, pituitary or hypothalamic disease, drugs and systemic conditions.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Clinical manifestations may resemble those of primary hypogonadism. A central defect beginning before or around puberty can cause delayed puberty with a eunuchoid phenotype. Headache or visual disturbance can suggest a pituitary cause.

subtypes.name: isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism [IHH]
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A central defect that may become apparent before or around puberty; listed variants include Normosmic IHH and Kallmann syndrome.

subtypes.name: Functional hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Secondary impairment associated with comorbidities or other potentially reversible influences, without an identified organic cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document testosterone deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain fasting morning measurements when compatible symptoms or signs are present, with confirmation of a pathological result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A low value requires assessment alongside gonadotropins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a central pattern of testosterone deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When pathological testosterone is detected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reduced or inappropriately normal gonadotropin levels support secondary hypogonadism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify hyperprolactinemia or another possible pituitary-related cause.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: With pathological testosterone, particularly when sexual desire is low or other suggestive findings are present.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated PRL may prompt pituitary imaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate an underlying pituitary lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: With elevated PRL, symptoms suggestive of a pituitary mass or another anterior pituitary hormone deficiency. Imaging is also suggested, on limited evidence, for severe disease with total testosterone < 6 nmol/L, 1.75 ng/mL and inadequate gonadotropins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible additional pituitary dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When pituitary symptoms occur or hyperprolactinemia is confirmed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess fertility wishes and possible congenital, medication-related, systemic or pituitary causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.

follow_up.schedule: If testosterone therapy is given, review initially at three months; monitor testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months and annually thereafter.
recommended_tests: Testosterone
Haematocrit
PSA
Digital rectal examination
long_term_effects: Testosterone therapy impairs spermatogenesis and is contraindicated when fertility is desired.
Monitor for elevated haematocrit during testosterone therapy.

conditions.name: Late onset hypogonadism
conditions.description: An adult-onset form of hypogonadism that may have an organic or functional cause and may be primary or secondary. Diagnosis requires persistent specific symptoms together with biochemical testosterone deficiency.
conditions.epidemiology: Prevalence rises with age and is particularly high among men with obesity, T2DM, MetS, CVD, COPD, renal disease or cancer. In men aged 40-79 years, reported incidence of symptomatic hypogonadism varies between 2.1 and 5.7%. In healthy ageing men up to 80 years, the gradual testosterone decline accounts for only a small proportion of cases. EMAS reported decreases of 0.4% per annum (log hormone-age) in total testosterone and 1.3% per annum in fT.
conditions.clinical_presentation: More specific sexual features include reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and fewer spontaneous or morning erections. Other sexual complaints include less frequent intercourse or masturbation and delayed ejaculation. Physical features include reduced vigorous activity, difficulty walking > 1 km, reduced bending, hot flushes, low energy and diminished physical strength or function. Psychological features include low mood, reduced motivation, fatigue, difficulties with concentration or memory, and disturbed sleep. These complaints are not individually specific and require clinical and biochemical interpretation.

subtypes.name: Functional hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Adult-onset disease associated chiefly with obesity and comorbidities, after exclusion of an organic cause.

subtypes.name: Classical hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Adult-onset disease may instead reflect an organic, structural or irreversible cause.

diagnostic_workup.test: History of symptoms, comorbidities, medicines and substances
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish a compatible clinical picture and identify influences on testosterone production or action; discuss fertility.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Evaluate symptomatic men rather than screening asymptomatic men systematically.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Headache or visual disturbance may indicate pituitary disease. Self-reported questionnaires and structured interviews have poor specificity and should not be used for systematic screening.

diagnostic_workup.test: body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess obesity and associated metabolic disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In all individuals undergoing assessment.

diagnostic_workup.test: Examination of testicular size, penile size and secondary sexual characteristics
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess overall androgen status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During physical examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm biochemical deficiency using a reliable assay.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Measure while fasting in the morning between 07.00 and 11.00 hours; repeat on at least two separate occasions when < 12 nmol/L and before initiating testosterone therapy. Avoid measurement during acute disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: 12 nmol/L (3.5 ng/mL) is a diagnostic threshold when compatible symptoms are present. Meta-analyses reported no treatment effect with baseline values > 12 nmol/L (3.5 ng/mL) and greater benefit with more severe deficiency, < 8 nmol/L.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure sex steroids.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When sex steroid assessment is undertaken.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Described as the most accurate method; standardised automated immuno-assays for total testosterone correlate well with it.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support calculated fT when total testosterone may not adequately reflect androgen status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider particularly when clinical conditions may alter SHBG.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Changes in SHBG can alter the interpretation of total testosterone.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further assess androgen status where SHBG may interfere with interpretation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when indicated by altered SHBG or an uncertain total testosterone result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Equilibrium dialysis is the most accurate measurement method; alternatively, calculate fT from SHBG and albumin. Direct fT assessment with available immuno-assays should be avoided. No clinically validated fT threshold is established, although EMAS data suggested < 220 pmol/L (6.4 ng/dL) could aid identification, especially when total testosterone is between 8.0 and 11 nmol/L.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate primary and secondary causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When pathological total testosterone is found.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated LH supports a primary cause; reduced or inappropriately normal LH supports a secondary cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a possible organic cause and investigate reduced sexual desire.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When pathological testosterone is detected or when low desire or other suggestive features occur.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Confirmed hyperprolactinemia calls for further pituitary assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible pituitary disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For secondary hypogonadism with elevated PRL, symptoms of a pituitary mass or another anterior pituitary hormone deficiency. Limited evidence also suggests MRI when total testosterone is < 6 nmol/L, 1.75 ng/mL with inadequate gonadotropins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible additional pituitary dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: With specific pituitary symptoms or confirmed hyperprolactinemia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify prostate abnormalities before testosterone therapy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before treatment and at least annually during treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A prostate abnormality may be present despite a normal PSA.

follow_up.schedule: After testosterone therapy begins, evaluate at three months; further clinical review may occur at six months or twelve months according to the patient and laboratory findings. Monitor testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months and annually thereafter. For polycythaemia vera or greater risk of raised haematocrit, evaluate every three months in the first year and at least every six months subsequently.
recommended_tests: Assess symptoms at baseline, three, six and twelve months and annually thereafter.
Measure BMI at baseline, twelve months and annually; measure waist circumference and blood pressure at baseline, three months, twelve months and annually.
Measure testosterone at baseline, three months, twelve months and annually.
Measure haematocrit and PSA at baseline, three months, six months, twelve months and annually, with the six-month table entries qualified for higher-risk groups and PCa survivors.
Perform DRE at baseline, twelve months and annually.
Assess lipid and glycaemic profile at baseline, twelve months and annually.
Consider DEXA at baseline and 18-24 months, particularly in more severe disease.
long_term_effects: Elevated haematocrit may emerge between three and twelve months after starting therapy or after subsequent treatment changes.
A haematocrit > 54% requires treatment adjustment or withdrawal and venesection when needed.
Monitor prostate findings and cardiovascular status where relevant.
Long-term cardiovascular outcomes beyond the available follow-up remain uncertain.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Discuss the appropriateness of PSA-based prostate screening and DRE during testosterone therapy with men aged < 40 or > 70 years.

conditions.name: Functional hypogonadism
conditions.description: Hypogonadism attributed mainly to comorbidities or other influences on the HPG axis without a recognised organic alteration. It is diagnosed after excluding a classical organic cause and may be potentially reversible.
conditions.epidemiology: Obesity and comorbidities account for most suggested cases; the contribution of ageing up to age 80 years appears relatively small.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Its testosterone-deficiency manifestations overlap with those of hypogonadism from organic causes; their severity can vary.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of comorbidities, drugs and substances
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify factors that may impair testosterone production or action.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An organic cause must be excluded before assigning a functional diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.test: body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess obesity, a frequent associated condition.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In all individuals undergoing evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish biochemical deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In symptomatic men, with fasting morning sampling and confirmation of a pathological result; avoid testing during acute illness.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Interpret with compatible symptoms and evaluation for an organic cause.

diagnostic_workup.test: luteinising hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and prolactin (PRL)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise the origin of deficiency and investigate possible organic causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When pathological total testosterone is detected.

diagnostic_workup.test: sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and free testosterone (fT)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify androgen status when SHBG may affect interpretation of total testosterone.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: There is no validated clinical fT threshold.

diagnostic_workup.test: Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and other pituitary hormone evaluations
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible organic pituitary cause.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When pituitary symptoms, elevated PRL or another anterior pituitary hormone deficiency warrant evaluation.

follow_up.schedule: If testosterone therapy is initiated, review at three months and monitor testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months, then annually.
recommended_tests: Consider glyco-metabolic profile assessment at baseline and at least annually.
Monitor testosterone, haematocrit, PSA and prostate findings during testosterone therapy.
long_term_effects: Monitor for elevated haematocrit and other treatment-related safety concerns.

conditions.name: Classical hypogonadism
conditions.description: Congenital or acquired disease causing structural or irreversible impairment of the pituitary gland, testes, or both.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Testosterone-deficiency effects overlap with functional hypogonadism; severity and phenotype can vary with the age when disease begins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify possible congenital, acquired, pituitary or testicular causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of hypogonadism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Earlier onset may change the clinical phenotype; headache or visual disturbance may suggest pituitary disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish biochemical deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain fasting morning samples and confirm a pathological result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Interpret in conjunction with symptoms, signs and gonadotropins.

diagnostic_workup.test: luteinising hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and prolactin (PRL)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate testicular from central disease and assess potential pituitary causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When testosterone is pathologically low.

diagnostic_workup.test: Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and other pituitary hormone evaluations
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected organic pituitary disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: With suggestive pituitary symptoms, elevated PRL or another anterior pituitary hormone deficiency.

follow_up.schedule: During testosterone therapy, initially review at three months and monitor testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months, then annually.
recommended_tests: Testosterone
Haematocrit
PSA
Digital rectal examination
long_term_effects: Monitor for elevated haematocrit and prostate abnormalities during testosterone therapy.

conditions.name: compensated or subclinical form of hypogonadism
conditions.description: A reported form with normal circulating testosterone and elevated LH; its clinical importance remains unclear.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the described hormonal pattern.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Testosterone is normal while LH is elevated.

conditions.name: ANDROGEN RESISTANCE/DECREASED TESTOSTERONE BIOACTIVITY
conditions.description: Conditions in which responsiveness to testosterone or its metabolites is reduced. The listed causes include congenital or developmental conditions and acquired factors affecting androgen-related activity.
conditions.clinical_presentation: When androgen insensitivity or a defect blocking androgen synthesis begins in foetal life, the phenotype may range from almost completely female to varying degrees of impaired virilisation.

subtypes.name: Partial or complete androgen insensitivity
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reduced responsiveness to androgens; complete insensitivity may cause an almost completely female phenotype after foetal-onset disease.

subtypes.name: Aromatase deficiency
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed among congenital or developmental causes of reduced testosterone bioactivity.

subtypes.name: 5α reductase type II (5aR) deficiency
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed among congenital or developmental causes.

subtypes.name: Kennedy diseases (spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed with other extensions of CAG repeats among congenital or developmental causes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the phenotype and identify possible congenital or acquired influences on androgen activity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When hypogonadism or reduced androgen activity is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Age at onset can substantially influence the phenotype.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify agents listed as interfering with androgen-related activity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of possible hypogonadism.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Extensions are listed alongside Kennedy diseases (spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy) among congenital or developmental causes of reduced androgen bioactivity.

conditions.name: Klinefelter syndrome
conditions.description: A trisomy associated with a 47,XXY karyotype and identified as a genetic cause of primary hypogonadism.
conditions.epidemiology: Global prevalence is 1/500-1,000 live male births; < 50% of affected individuals receive a diagnosis during their lifetime.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A peripheral defect presenting before or around puberty may be accompanied by delayed puberty and an overall eunuchoid phenotype.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess delayed puberty and body proportions suggestive of an early-onset hypogonadal phenotype.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When an early-onset peripheral defect is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.test: serum total testosterone, luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess testosterone deficiency and distinguish primary from secondary hypogonadism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of suspected hypogonadism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated LH supports a primary pattern.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: The karyotype associated with Klinefelter syndrome.

recommendations.statement: Identify coexisting illnesses, medications and substances that may affect testosterone production or action.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Obtain total testosterone between 07.00 and 11.00 hours while the patient is fasting, using a dependable laboratory assay.
recommendations.rationale: Food intake and circadian variation can affect testosterone measurements.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: When total testosterone is < 12 nmol/L, repeat the measurement on at least two separate occasions before initiating testosterone therapy.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Apply total testosterone of 12 nmol/L (3.5 ng/mL) as a reliable diagnostic threshold for late onset hypogonadism (LOH).
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: When indicated, measure sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and calculate free testosterone.
recommendations.rationale: Conditions that alter SHBG may change total testosterone values in relation to actual androgen levels.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Assess serum luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) to distinguish types of hypogonadism.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Measure prolactin (PRL) when reduced sexual desire, or other suggestive signs or symptoms, occurs alongside secondary hypogonadism.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Obtain pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in secondary hypogonadism when PRL is elevated, symptoms suggest a pituitary mass, and/or another anterior pituitary hormone deficiency is present.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Obtain pituitary MRI in severe secondary hypogonadism when total testosterone is < 6 nmol/L.
recommendations.rationale: The evidence supporting imaging in severe hypogonadism with inadequate gonadotropin levels is limited.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Limit screening for LOH to men who have symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Do not use structured interviews or self-reported questionnaires for routine LOH screening.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH

recommendations.statement: Do not administer testosterone therapy to eugonadal men.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence does not show a benefit for sexual dysfunction in eugonadal men.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.2.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for testosterone therapy outcome

recommendations.statement: Provide testosterone therapy as the initial treatment for hypogonadal patients with mild erectile dysfunction (ED).
recommendations.rationale: Testosterone therapy alone produced a clinically effective result in patients with milder ED.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.2.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for testosterone therapy outcome

recommendations.statement: For more severe ED, combine phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors with testosterone therapy.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.2.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for testosterone therapy outcome

recommendations.statement: Treat severe depressive symptoms and osteoporosis with conventional medical therapies.
recommendations.rationale: The document does not establish testosterone therapy alone as effective for most clinical depressive disorders or for reducing fracture risk.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.2.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for testosterone therapy outcome

recommendations.statement: Do not prescribe testosterone therapy for weight reduction or improvement of cardio-metabolic status.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence concerning weight and metabolic outcomes is conflicting.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.2.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for testosterone therapy outcome

recommendations.statement: Do not use testosterone therapy to improve cognition, vitality or physical strength in ageing men.
recommendations.rationale: The reported evidence does not establish a meaningful benefit for these outcomes.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.2.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for testosterone therapy outcome

recommendations.statement: Treat organic causes of hypogonadism, such as pituitary masses or hyperprolactinemia, when indicated.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for choice of treatment for LOH

recommendations.statement: Before initiating testosterone therapy, improve lifestyle and reduce excess weight, discontinue medications that impair testosterone production when feasible, and treat other co-morbidities when possible.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for choice of treatment for LOH

recommendations.statement: Explain the anticipated benefits and adverse effects of each treatment option thoroughly, and choose the testosterone preparation jointly with the fully informed patient.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for choice of treatment for LOH

recommendations.statement: When beginning treatment in high-risk men, favour testosterone gels over long-acting depot preparations.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for choice of treatment for LOH

recommendations.statement: Before considering testosterone therapy for symptomatic hypogonadal men surgically treated for localised prostate cancer (PCa) who have no evidence of active disease, counsel them fully about the insufficient long-term safety data.
recommendations.rationale: Long-term prospective safety data for PCa survivors are insufficient.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: Limit testosterone therapy after PCa treatment to patients at low risk of recurrent PCa, starting only after at least one year follow-up with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) < 0.01 ng/mL.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: Tell patients treated for breast cancer that the safety of testosterone therapy in this group is unknown.
recommendations.rationale: Information on testosterone therapy following successful treatment of male breast cancer is unavailable.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: Evaluate cardiovascular risk factors before initiating testosterone therapy.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: Before testosterone therapy, assess cardiovascular symptoms in men with established cardiovascular disease (CVD), and provide close clinical assessment and evaluation during treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: If testosterone therapy is needed for men with hypogonadism and pre-existing CVD, venous-thromboembolism or chronic cardiac failure, treat cautiously with careful clinical monitoring and regular testosterone and haematocrit measurements, keeping haematocrit from exceeding 54%.
recommendations.context: Pre-existing cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease or chronic cardiac failure
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: Check for a family history of venous-thromboembolism before commencing testosterone therapy.
recommendations.rationale: A positive family history warrants investigation for an unrecognised thrombophilia-hypofibrinolysis condition.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: Measure testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months after starting testosterone therapy and annually thereafter. If haematocrit is > 54%, adjust or stop treatment and perform venesection if necessary. Once haematocrit normalises, restart at a lower dose and consider a topical testosterone preparation.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: Assess patients with polycythaemia vera or increased risk of elevated haematocrit every three months during the first year of testosterone therapy and at least every six months thereafter.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

recommendations.statement: For PCa survivors receiving testosterone therapy, measure total PSA at three, six and twelve months in the first year and annually afterward.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment

special_populations.population: Men with obesity or metabolic disorders
special_populations.considerations: Low testosterone is common in men with obesity, MetS and T2DM. Obesity and associated illness can contribute to functional hypogonadism. Weight loss and physical activity may raise testosterone levels, although the reported increase is small. In men with ED, metabolic comorbidity may lessen improvement in sexual function with testosterone therapy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For overweight or obese men with hypogonadism, use weight loss and lifestyle changes as the initial approach. Address co-morbidities before starting testosterone therapy when possible. Men with T2DM and persistent sexual difficulties may require concomitant PDE5Is.

special_populations.considerations: This diagnosis requires exclusion of a classical organic cause. Co-morbidities or concomitant drugs may impair testosterone production, and suppression of the HPG axis may be reversible.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Treat underlying conditions and withdraw drugs that impair testosterone production when possible before starting testosterone therapy. Anti-oestrogens have been suggested as off-label options for functional secondary hypogonadism, but the evidence is poor; they require an intact HPG axis.

special_populations.population: Men with secondary hypogonadism who desire fertility
special_populations.considerations: Exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotropin secretion and impairs spermatogenesis. In secondary hypogonadism, gonadotropin treatment may restore sperm production as well as testosterone levels.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use testosterone therapy in men seeking fertility treatment. Consider gonadotropin therapy; the guideline identifies combined hCG and FSH as producing better outcomes than hCG alone.

special_populations.population: Men with primary hypogonadism who desire fertility
special_populations.considerations: The guideline distinguishes primary hypogonadism from secondary hypogonadism: in primary hypogonadism, it states that only testosterone therapy can be considered, while noting that this treatment can impair fertility through suppression of the HPT axis.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Testosterone therapy is contraindicated in individuals who desire fertility.

special_populations.considerations: Studies have reported either recovery or persistent reduction of testosterone levels after COVID-19; one longitudinal study observed further improvement up to twelve months after infection. Whether low testosterone directly worsens COVID-19 outcomes remains under investigation.

special_populations.population: Men with active or previously treated male breast cancer
special_populations.considerations: The guideline identifies male breast cancer as a contraindication to testosterone therapy. It states that safety information for testosterone therapy after successful breast cancer treatment is unavailable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use testosterone therapy in men with active or treated male breast cancer.

special_populations.population: Men with active advanced prostate cancer or a history of treated localised prostate cancer
special_populations.considerations: Testosterone therapy must be avoided in advanced PCa. For men previously treated for localised PCa, long-term safety regarding recurrence and progression has not been established; the guideline calls for counselling about this uncertainty.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Limit consideration of testosterone therapy after surgical treatment of localised PCa to men at low risk of recurrence, without evidence of active disease, after at least one year follow-up and with PSA < 0.01 ng/mL. Measure total PSA at three, six and twelve months during the first treatment year and annually thereafter.

special_populations.population: Men with severe lower urinary tract symptoms
special_populations.considerations: Severe LUTS, defined by IPSS score > 19, is a relative contraindication to testosterone therapy because these patients have generally been excluded from RCTs, leaving limited long-term safety information.

special_populations.population: Men with pre-existing CVD or elevated cardiovascular risk
special_populations.considerations: Hypogonadism and ED may coexist with underlying CVD. The guideline advises assessment of cardiovascular risk factors before testosterone therapy and close clinical evaluation during treatment for men with known CVD.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: When testosterone therapy is required in men with pre-existing CVD, use caution and regularly measure testosterone and haematocrit, keeping haematocrit from exceeding 54%.

special_populations.considerations: Fluid retention during testosterone therapy may exacerbate severe chronic cardiac failure. The guideline identifies uncontrolled or poorly controlled congestive heart failure as an absolute contraindication.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use testosterone therapy in severe chronic cardiac failure. If treatment is undertaken in a man with chronic cardiac failure, provide careful clinical follow-up and regular testosterone and haematocrit measurements.

special_populations.population: Men with venous-thromboembolism or a family history of venous-thromboembolism
special_populations.considerations: A positive family history warrants investigation for possible undiagnosed thrombophilia-hypofibrinolysis and counselling before testosterone therapy. Men with pre-existing venous-thromboembolism require caution if treatment is needed.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: If testosterone therapy is required in a man with pre-existing venous-thromboembolism, monitor clinically and measure testosterone and haematocrit regularly, without allowing haematocrit to exceed 54%.

special_populations.population: Men with polycythaemia vera or increased risk of elevated haematocrit
special_populations.considerations: A high baseline haematocrit, smoking and respiratory conditions increase concern for erythrocytosis during testosterone therapy. The guideline also highlights COPD, OSAS, morbid obesity and residence at high altitude. Haematocrit ≥ 54% is listed as an absolute contraindication to starting testosterone therapy, while a baseline value of 48-50% warrants careful evaluation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Evaluate men with polycythaemia vera or increased erythrocytosis risk every three months during the first year of testosterone therapy and at least every six months thereafter. If haematocrit exceeds 54%, adjust or withdraw treatment and use venesection if required; after normalisation, reintroduce testosterone therapy at a lower dose and consider a topical preparation.

special_populations.considerations: The guideline reports no evidence that testosterone therapy causes sleep apnoea or worsens it. It also identifies sleep apnoea as a risk factor for elevated haematocrit during treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For men at increased risk of elevated haematocrit, apply the guideline's closer haematocrit monitoring schedule during testosterone therapy.

special_populations.population: Hypogonadal men at high risk of bone fractures
special_populations.considerations: Severe hypogonadism is frequently associated with bone loss, but available evidence is insufficient to establish whether testosterone therapy alone reduces fracture risk.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use antiresorptive therapy as the first-choice treatment. Offer its combination with testosterone therapy only when hypogonadism-related symptoms are present.

special_populations.population: Men aged < 40 or > 70 years receiving testosterone therapy
special_populations.considerations: The guideline notes a low risk of PCa in men aged < 40 years and states that PCa mortality risk in men aged > 70 years has not warranted monitoring in the general population.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Discuss PSA and DRE screening during testosterone therapy with men in these age groups.

special_populations.population: Men with congenital or pre-pubertal hypogonadism
special_populations.considerations: The age at which hypogonadism begins affects its presentation. Foetal onset may cause defects in virilisation, while pre- or peripubertal onset may present with delayed puberty and a eunuchoid phenotype.
The guideline distinguishes men at higher treatment risk when choosing an initial testosterone preparation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use testosterone gels rather than long-acting depot administration when initiating treatment.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Methods
document_sections.content: For the 2025 Sexual and Reproductive Health Guidelines, the panels systematically identified and assessed new evidence for Sections 5 Management of Erectile Dysfunction and 11 Male Infertility. Searches of Medline, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Libraries covered the period between the 1st Jan 2023 and 1st May 2024. Screening included 1,499 unique records for Section 5 and 2,788 for Section 11. The panels formulate recommendations around important clinical decisions. Strength ratings consider evidence quality and certainty, effect size, the balance of benefits and harms, and patient values and preferences. Strong recommendations generally reflect higher-quality evidence and/or a favourable benefit–harm balance and patient preference. Weak recommendations generally reflect lower-quality evidence, an uncertain benefit–harm balance, and/or variable or uncertain preferences.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Review
document_sections.content: The EAU Sexual and Reproductive Health Guidelines underwent peer review before their 2020 publication. The priapism section was reviewed before publication in 2021, and the section on penile size abnormalities and dysmorphophobia was reviewed before publication in 2023.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.1 Definition
document_sections.content: Male hypogonadism combines symptoms, with or without signs, and biochemical testosterone deficiency. It involves reduced testicular androgen production and/or impaired sperm production. Causes include primary testicular dysfunction, inadequate hypothalamic-pituitary stimulation, and, less commonly, reduced cellular responsiveness to testosterone at the androgen receptor. Multiple organs and QoL may be affected. The chapter focuses on adult male hypogonadism, also termed late onset hypogonadism (LOH), while addressing some congenital and pre-pubertal presentations.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.2 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: LOH becomes more prevalent with age, chiefly in association with obesity, comorbidities such as diabetes, and poor overall health. Reported hypogonadism incidence is between 12.3 and 11.7 cases per 1,000 people per year; among men aged 40-79 years, symptomatic hypogonadism incidence varies between 2.1 and 5.7%. Healthy ageing alone contributes relatively little: testosterone declines only gradually up to the age of 80 years. LOH is particularly prevalent in men with obesity, T2DM, MetS, CVD, COPD, renal disease, or cancer. Low testosterone is relatively common with T2DM and metabolic derangements. Klinefelter syndrome, associated with a 47,XXY karyotype, is the most prevalent genetic cause of primary hypogonadism; its global prevalence is 1/500-1,000 live male births, yet < 50% of affected individuals receive a diagnosis during life.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.3 Classification
document_sections.content: Aetiological classification distinguishes primary from secondary hypogonadism. A compensated or subclinical form has normal serum testosterone with elevated LH, but its clinical importance remains uncertain. Classical/ Organic hypogonadism involves congenital or acquired structural and/or irreversible pituitary or testicular disease. Functional hypogonadism lacks a recognised organic HPG-axis lesion, usually arises with comorbidity, and calls first for improvement or resolution of the underlying condition. Labelling all functional cases LOH is incorrect. LOH encompasses adult-onset organic or functional disease of either primary or secondary origin; its definition requires persistent specific symptoms plus biochemical testosterone deficiency. Testosterone deficiency can also arise through reduced sensitivity to testosterone or its metabolites. Classification helps select therapy: appropriate treatment of secondary hypogonadism can theoretically restore both testosterone and fertility, whereas primary hypogonadism permits consideration of testosterone therapy, which may impair fertility through HPT-axis suppression. Symptoms can be similar regardless of disease origin, but onset influences phenotype. Foetal-onset disease may produce an almost complete female phenotype or varying virilisation defects; pre- or peripubertal disease may cause delayed puberty and a eunuchoid phenotype; post-pubertal disease, particularly with ageing, may produce mild symptoms mistaken for ageing.

It distinguishes common from uncommon causes where indicated.
