document_sections.heading: 3.2.1 Obesity
document_sections.content: Low testosterone is common with obesity. Compared with men whose testosterone is adequate, hypogonadal men have a greater fat-mass percentage and less lean mass. Low testosterone is strongly associated with visceral fat accumulation, lipid deposition in liver and muscle, and atherosclerosis.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2 Metabolic Syndrome/Type 2 Diabetes
document_sections.content: Hypogonadism commonly accompanies MetS or its components: central obesity, hyperglycaemia, insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, and arterial hypertension. Several RCTs indicate that testosterone therapy may improve insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia and reduce total and LDL-cholesterol. Some RCTs and registry studies in hypogonadal men with T2DM found better glycaemic control, but the evidence is inconclusive. In a placebo-controlled RCT of 1,007 men with impaired glucose tolerance or newly diagnosed T2DM and total testosterone < 14 nmol/L, two years of therapy reduced the proportion with T2DM regardless of a lifestyle programme. A registry study associated therapy over time with T2DM remission. HDL-cholesterol may fall, remain stable, or rise. Studies report lower mortality among treated than untreated men with MetS and low testosterone, without conclusive evidence. ED affects up to 70% of men with MetS and T2DM; its causes are multifactorial, and 30% of men with ED also have testosterone deficiency/hypogonadism. Some evidence suggests that, in T2DM, ED occurs only with clearly reduced testosterone (< 8 nmol/L or 2.31 ng/mL); vascular and neuropathic disease has been proposed as the predominant explanation. Men presenting with ED should be screened for MetS, and testosterone measurement may be offered to those with ED and diabetes. Placebo-controlled RCTs in T2DM showed improvements in desire and satisfaction, but not erectile function; a meta-analysis reported similar findings. Conversely, a large two-year RCT in men with impaired glucose tolerance or newly diagnosed T2DM and low testosterone (< 14 nmol/L) found significantly better sexual function and ED with testosterone undecanoate than placebo. Testosterone therapy has also been associated with less body fat and more lean mass. An eleven-year registry study associated long-acting intramuscular testosterone undecanoate with substantial, gradual weight loss and reduced waist circumference.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3 Sars-CoV-2 / COVID-19
document_sections.content: Studies suggest that low circulating testosterone occurs more often alongside worse COVID-19 outcomes. A cohort analysis of 723 men with previous COVID-19 associated hypogonadism with greater hospitalisation risk. A meta-analysis linked low testosterone at hospital admission to a four- to five-fold greater adjusted risk of ICU admission or death. The role of testosterone therapy during acute disease is unknown. In one study, treated hypogonadal patients had lower hospitalisation risk after SARS-CoV-2 infection, but whether low testosterone directly worsens outcomes remains under investigation. An adaptive reduction in testosterone-dependent activities during acute infection cannot be excluded. A meta-analysis found secondary or mixed hypogonadism more frequently during acute infection. Recovery studies have reported either restored testosterone or persistently low levels in the majority of cases; a longitudinal study observed further improvement up to twelve months after COVID-19. Men recovering from COVID-19 should be followed to exclude long-term effects on sperm and testosterone production.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Late-onset hypogonadism
document_sections.content: Testosterone production decreases with age. EMAS reported annual declines of 0.4% in total testosterone and 1.3% in fT. Adult comorbidities can disrupt the HPG axis, causing primary or, more commonly, secondary hypogonadism and materially altering age-related decline. Combined MMAS waves associated comorbidity and obesity with significantly lower total, free, and bio-available testosterone; smoking tended to raise these measures. EMAS supported those observations. Functional hypogonadism is diagnosed after excluding a classical organic cause. Its proposed principal causes are obesity, comorbidity, and ageing, with obesity and comorbidity accounting for most cases. Chronic inflammatory cytokines, and obesity-related adipocytokines and E2, can suppress the HPG axis; ageing contributes relatively little up to age 80 years. Because functional suppression may reverse with measures such as weight loss, the need for testosterone therapy has been questioned. The functional–organic distinction remains debated: symptomatic low testosterone reflects an HPT-axis disorder even when no identifiable pathological cause is found.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1 Clinical Diagnosis and Evaluation
document_sections.content: LOH diagnosis depends on compatible signs and symptoms together with low morning serum total testosterone on two or more occasions, using a reliable assay under fasting conditions.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2 History taking
document_sections.content: Symptoms associated with LOH are nonspecific and require interpretation alongside clinical and biochemical findings. Questionnaires and structured interviews may support biochemical diagnosis or assessment of treatment outcomes, but poor specificity precludes their use for systematic screening. Headache or visual disturbance may suggest pituitary disease. Previous surgery for cryptorchidism or hypospadias may indicate a congenital defect. Every patient needs assessment for chronic and systemic comorbidity and drugs that could interfere with the HPG axis; fertility should always be discussed. Acute illness can cause functional hypogonadism, so serum total testosterone determination should be avoided during such illness, although testosterone's role in this setting remains unclear.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.3 Physical examination
document_sections.content: BMI determination and waist measurement are strongly recommended for everyone because obesity, often associated with functional hypogonadism, is common. Testicular and penile size and secondary sexual characteristics inform androgen-status assessment. An upper segment/lower segment ratio (n.v. > 0.92) and arm-span to height ratio (n.v. < 1.0) may help recognise eunuchoid body shape, particularly with pre-pubertal hypogonadism or delayed puberty. DRE should be performed to identify prostate abnormalities before any testosterone therapy or, when prostate volume is reduced, to support suspicion of hypogonadism.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.4 Laboratory Diagnostics
document_sections.content: Circadian variation and food intake can affect testosterone. Measure fasting serum total testosterone in the morning, between 07.00 and 11.00 hours, and confirm an initially pathological result before treatment. LC-MS/MS is the most accurate sex-steroid method; standardised automated total-testosterone immuno-assays correlate well with it. Immuno-assays do not accurately estimate fT directly, so that approach is not recommended and should be avoided. Equilibrium dialysis is most accurate for fT; alternatively, calculate fT using SHBG and albumin. Total testosterone varies with SHBG. Meta-analyses found testosterone therapy ineffective when baseline testosterone is > 12 nmol/L (3.5 ng/mL), with positive outcomes below < 12 nmol/L and greater benefit in symptomatic patients below < 8 nmol/L. A level of 12 nmol/L is therefore a possible treatment threshold when symptoms are present. Consider fT when conditions affect SHBG, although clinical studies provide no validated fT threshold. EMAS data suggest fT < 220 pmol/L (6.4 ng/dL) improves identification, particularly when total testosterone is between 8.0 and 11 nmol/L. When total testosterone is pathological, determine LH with PRL to clarify the cause and exclude possible organic disease; FSH and LH further distinguish primary from secondary hypogonadism. PRL can also be considered first-line screening for reduced desire. Contrast-enhanced pituitary MRI and other pituitary hormone testing are required with visual disturbance, headache, or confirmed hyperprolactinemia. Limited evidence also supports considering MRI when testosterone is < 6 nmol/L, 1.75 ng/mL and gonadotropins are inadequate.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation and screening of LOH
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries state that sexual symptoms are most specific for LOH (LE 1a); diagnosis combines specific androgen-deficiency manifestations with consistently low testosterone (LE 1a); total testosterone 12 nmol/L (3.5 ng/mL) is a reliable diagnostic threshold (LE 1a); functional hypogonadism related to comorbidity or drugs is diagnosed after organic causes are excluded (LE 4); calculated free testosterone < 220 pmol/L is a suggested possible cut-off (LE 3); and screening questionnaires or interviews have poor specificity (LE 2a). Strong recommendations are to identify diseases, drugs, and substances affecting testosterone production or action; measure fasting morning total testosterone at 07.00 and 11.00 hours with a reliable assay; repeat total testosterone on at least two separate occasions if < 12 nmol/L and before therapy; use 12 nmol/L total testosterone (3.5 ng/mL) as the LOH threshold; measure SHBG and calculate free testosterone when indicated; obtain LH and FSH to distinguish hypogonadism types; measure PRL when low desire or other suggestive features coexist with secondary hypogonadism; obtain pituitary MRI in secondary hypogonadism with elevated PRL, pituitary-mass symptoms, and/or another anterior pituitary hormone deficiency; screen only symptomatic men; and avoid systematic LOH screening with structured interviews or self-reported questionnaires. A Weak recommendation supports pituitary MRI in severe secondary hypogonadism with total testosterone < 6 nmol/L.

document_sections.content: The diagnostic diagram begins with compatible symptoms and signs, then checks interfering drugs or substances, metabolic disease, and possible testosterone-therapy contraindications. It directs fasting morning total testosterone measurement (7-11 am), with PRL, SHBG, calculated free testosterone, or LH assessment as indicated. It distinguishes TT > 12 nM with reduced cFT, for which hypogonadism remains possible; TT > 12 nM, for which it is unlikely; and TT < 12 nM, for which it is possible. Repeat testing with LH, PRL, and, where applicable, SHBG and cFT helps distinguish secondary disease with reduced or inappropriately normal LH from primary disease with elevated LH. For secondary disease, the diagram considers interfering exposures and metabolic conditions and indicates pituitary MRI with TT < 6 nM, elevated PRL, headache, or visual disturbance. It also depicts TT < 8 nM, assessment of reversible contributors and fertility wishes, gonadotropin therapy when fertility is desired, and a possible testosterone-therapy trial after contraindications are excluded.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.1 Indications and contraindications for treatment of hypogonadism
document_sections.content: Symptomatic patients with total testosterone < 12 nmol/L may receive testosterone therapy if no specific contraindication applies. Untreated breast cancer and PCa are absolute contraindications; cardiovascular events and uncontrolled or poorly controlled congestive heart failure also require consideration. Severe LUTS with IPSS > 19 is a relative contraindication because long-term treatment data are insufficient. A family history of venous thromboembolism warrants investigation for unrecognised thrombophilia-hypofibrinolysis and counselling. At HCT > 54%, clinical circumstances may require treatment withdrawal, dose reduction, formulation change, or venesection to avoid potential cardiovascular complications. Baseline HTC of 48-50% needs careful assessment, particularly with COPD, OSAS, or residence at high altitude. The Framingham Heart Study associated HCT > 48% with greater CAD and mortality risk and with cardiovascular disorders. Testosterone therapy suppresses gonadotropins, endogenous testosterone, and spermatogenesis; it is contraindicated when fertility is desired. In secondary hypogonadism with low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins, FSH and LH analogues can replace the deficiency when fertility is sought.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.1 Sexual dysfunction
document_sections.content: Sexual concerns predominate in hypogonadism. Evidence suggests testosterone therapy may benefit sexual functioning when total testosterone is < 12 nmol/L; benefit for sexual dysfunction in eugonadal men has not been demonstrated. Normalising testosterone appears more relevant than formulation choice. A placebo-controlled RCT meta-analysis found significantly better IIEF erectile-function scores, with greater improvement at total testosterone < 8 nmol/L than in milder hypogonadism at < 12 nmol/L. Desire showed a similar pattern, while diabetes or obesity attenuated improvement. Testosterone alone achieved clinically effective results only with milder ED; an updated analysis supported these findings. In TRAVERSE, gel treatment for two years improved sexual activity, symptoms, and desire—but not erectile function—in middle-aged and older men with total testosterone < 10.4 nmol/L and established or high CVD risk. Meta-analyses also found improvements in intercourse, orgasm, and overall satisfaction versus placebo. Men with T2DM generally have modest sexual improvement and may need PDE5Is. A meta-analysis of 913 patients from eight RCTs suggested testosterone plus PDE5Is improved erectile function more than PDE5Is alone, although the combination's specific benefit is unclear; evidence for combining testosterone with other ED drugs is lacking. In the TTrials Sexual Function Trial, older men aged ≥ 65 years improved on 10 of 12 sexual-activity measures, especially intercourse, masturbation, and nocturnal erections. Improvement tracked increases in total testosterone, fT, and E2, without an established threshold. A study of 220 men with MetS, with or without T2DM, found better sexual function among those reporting sexual problems, including improved IIEF scores, libido, and satisfaction.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.2 Vitality and physical strength
document_sections.content: Testosterone stimulates muscle growth and strength, and AAS have been used to enhance competitive-sport performance. In hypogonadal men, testosterone therapy increases muscle mass and decreases fat mass but has limited effect on final weight. Its value for older men with restricted mobility remains uncertain. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 1999-2004 found no overall association between testosterone and physical activity; among non-obese men, however, those in the highest activity tertile were significantly less likely to have low or low-normal testosterone than those in the lowest tertile. In the TTrials physical-function cohort, treatment did not substantially improve the proportion whose 6-minute walk increased > 50 m or the absolute distance gained. Across the entire TTrials population, both outcomes improved significantly but modestly; the Vitality Trial produced similar findings. A meta-analysis of 2043 people older than 60 years found no significant muscle-strength improvement versus placebo.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.3 Mood and cognition
document_sections.content: Observational studies associate hypogonadism with depressive symptoms and poorer QoL, but its relationship to depression incidence is uncertain. Few placebo-controlled RCTs address depression. TTrials found modest improvements in continuously measured mood and depressive symptoms. A meta-analysis of 1,890 hypogonadal men with baseline total testosterone < 12 nmol/L or fT < 225 pmol/L from 27 RCTs found benefit particularly with milder symptoms. In BLAST, men with T2DM and depression were less likely than those without depression to improve in sexual-dysfunction symptoms. TRAVERSE findings suggest testosterone alone is not an effective option for most men with clinical depressive disorders. Robust QoL evidence is limited: meta-analyses suggest a statistically significant but small and heterogeneous effect versus placebo. Cognitive effects are still less certain. TTrials found no cognitive benefit in 493 people with age-associated memory impairment. A meta-analysis of 17 studies involving 1,438 patients, mean age 70.4 years and mean follow-up 45.6 weeks, likewise found no effect on cognitive domains.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.4 Body composition and metabolic profile
document_sections.content: LOH is associated with more fat and less lean mass, especially visceral adiposity, alongside lipid accumulation in liver and muscle and atherosclerosis. Some studies suggest testosterone therapy reduces body-fat percentage and increases lean mass; reported declines in waist circumference, weight, and BMI are more pronounced after twelve months. In the two-year T4DM RCT, testosterone plus a lifestyle programme reduced waist circumference and total and abdominal fat more than lifestyle measures alone, while increasing total and arm muscle mass and non-dominant-hand strength. Weight reduction approached but did not reach significance, potentially because muscle gain offset fat loss. Earlier observational and registry evidence is limited by non-random treatment assignment and possible selection bias. RCT evidence instead shows comparable changes in fat and lean mass without a weight change. A meta-analysis of seventeen RCTs in T2DM and/or MetS found better body composition without weight change, favourable fasting glycaemia and HOMA results, and conflicting HbA1c and lipid results. T4DM findings indicate reduced T2DM incidence at follow-up with combined lifestyle measures and therapy. Conversely, a TRAVERSE subgroup analysis found no glycaemic-control improvement in men with hypogonadism and prediabetes or diabetes; population differences and the absence of a specific lifestyle programme may partly explain the neutral result.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.5 Bone
document_sections.content: Normal-range circulating sex steroids appear necessary for bone mineralisation. The association of mild hypogonadism with osteopenia or osteoporosis is weak, whereas severe deficiency at total testosterone < 3.5 nM commonly accompanies bone loss and osteoporosis regardless of age. Three meta-analyses found higher BMD with testosterone therapy, with the largest effect at the lumber level; the latter analysis found an even greater BMD effect among patients with diabetes. TTrials and T4DM also reported increased BMD in ageing hypogonadal men. In a TRAVERSE subgroup, overall fracture incidence was numerically higher with testosterone than placebo, but fractures were not the primary study outcome; bone and hip fractures did not differ. Evidence is insufficient to establish whether testosterone alone changes fracture risk, and its adjunctive use with antiresorptive treatment in patients at high fracture risk is unestablished. Antiresorptive treatment must be first choice for hypogonadal men at high fracture risk; combining it with testosterone should be offered only when hypogonadism-related symptoms are also present.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for testosterone therapy outcome
document_sections.content: The evidence summary reports possible improvements in mild ED and libido among hypogonadal men (LE 1a), other sexual symptoms (LE 1b), body composition and insulin resistance (LE 1a), weight, waist circumference, and lipid profile despite conflicting evidence (LE 3), mild depressive symptoms (LE 1a), and BMD despite inadequate fracture-risk information (LE 1a). Strong recommendations are not to treat eugonadal men with testosterone; to use testosterone first-line for hypogonadal patients with mild ED; to use conventional medical treatment for severe depressive symptoms and osteoporosis; and not to use testosterone to improve cognition, vitality, or physical strength in ageing men. Weak recommendations are to combine PDE5Is with testosterone for more severe ED and not to use testosterone for weight reduction or improvement of cardio-metabolic status.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.1 Lifestyle factors
document_sections.content: Functional hypogonadism commonly coexists with obesity and metabolic disease. Weight loss and lifestyle changes should be the initial approach in overweight or obese hypogonadal men. A meta-analysis found that a low-calorie diet can reverse obesity-associated secondary hypogonadism by raising total testosterone and fT, lowering oestrogens, and normalising gonadotropins; an updated analysis linked testosterone increase significantly to weight reduction. Exercise can have similar effects associated with exercise duration and weight loss. Testosterone gains from diet and exercise are small (1-2 nmol). Weight regain reaches 60-86% after three years and 75-121% after five years. Lifestyle change remains essential for obesity management. Some evidence suggests treated obese men obtain greater relief of testosterone-deficiency symptoms than men receiving lifestyle changes alone; evidence for additional benefit from combining lifestyle intervention and testosterone therapy remains limited. Over two years, T4DM found greater reductions in waist circumference and total and abdominal fat with combined therapy than with lifestyle intervention alone, but no significant additional body-weight reduction.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2 Medical preparations
document_sections.content: Several testosterone formulations are available, but direct product comparisons are lacking. Patients should receive information on each preparation's potential benefits and risks. Formulation choice should reflect the clinical situation, availability, and patient needs and expectations.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2.1 Oral formulations
document_sections.content: An oral TU formulation introduced in the 1970s was reformulated with castor oil and propylene glycol laureate to permit room-temperature storage. Its principal limitation is low bioavailability that depends strongly on dietary fat. The FDA approved a liquid-filled soft-gel oral TU with improved availability and later approved another oral formulation using Vitamin E, phytosterol esters, polyoxyl 40 hydrogenated castor oil, and propylene glycol monolaurate as carriers. TU capsules achieved steady 24-hour mean serum testosterone in more than 80% of hypogonadal men and significantly improved sexual-function domains against baseline at all measured times, with an excellent reported safety profile. All newer oral TU formulations have been associated with a mild blood-pressure increase and carry an FDA black-box warning about this risk. Mesterolone, an orally administered 5α-DHT derivative, cannot be converted to oestrogens. Its restricted bioactivity limits long-term use; it may be used only briefly for specific indications such as painful gynaecomastia.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2.2 Parenteral formulations
document_sections.content: Injectable preparations differ by half-life. Testosterone propionate requires frequent divided injections, usually 50 mg every two to three days. Cypionate and enanthate-T require dosing every two to four weeks. A mixed-ester formulation containing TU, isocaproate, phenyl propionate, and propionate is available in some countries and provides steadier release. Older injectable formulations can nevertheless cause wide testosterone fluctuations that patients may find unpleasant and that may contribute to effects such as polycythaemia. Longer-acting injectable TU has a favourable reported benefit–safety profile: 1,000 mg is given initially every twelve weeks following a six-week loading dose; after three to five injections, the interval may be adjusted to ten to fourteen weeks using pre-injection concentrations to maintain levels usually > 12 and < 18 nmol/L.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2.3 Transdermal testosterone preparations
document_sections.content: Testosterone gels are the most commonly used transdermal preparations. After one daily application, absorption through the stratum corneum establishes a subcutaneous reservoir that releases testosterone for 24 hours; gels can normalise serum levels with a favourable reported safety profile. Devices and penetration enhancers may reduce adverse effects. Skin reactions are less prominent than with traditional patches, but close skin contact can transfer testosterone; clothing or application to a less-contacted site can reduce this risk. Gel formulations of 1.62-2% reduce the applied quantity and skin residue. An alcohol-based underarm testosterone (2%) solution is applied once daily using a metered device and is unavailable in Europe. Monitor testosterone to optimise dose; sampling two to four hours after gel application captures the absorbed peak. Repeat testing may be appropriate when results vary or gel contamination near the venepuncture site falsely raises a result. Hydroalcoholic DHT 2.5% gel is available in some European countries and reaches steady state in two to three days. It is not aromatised and may help with specific conditions such as gynaecomastia or microphallus.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2.4 Transmucosal formulations
document_sections.content: A sustained-release mucoadhesive testosterone buccal tablet remains available in several countries. It is placed against the upper gums twice daily and removed after 12 hours because it does not dissolve fully. It can restore physiological testosterone with usually minimal or transient local effects, including gum oedema, blistering, and gingivitis. Intranasal testosterone gel, available in countries including the USA and Canada, uses a metered pump two or three times daily. It is rapid and non-invasive and avoids transfer to other people associated with some topical products. Preliminary evidence suggests less gonadotropin suppression and lower haematocrit-increase risk.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2.5 Subdermal depots
document_sections.content: Implanted testosterone pellets, available in relatively few countries, last four to seven months—the longest duration among the described formulations—but implantation is invasive and may be unacceptable to some patients.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2.6 Anti-oestrogens
document_sections.content: SERMs and AI have been proposed off-label to restore testosterone and fertility in functional secondary hypogonadism or idiopathic infertility. By preventing oestrogen-mediated HPG-axis down-regulation, they may be particularly useful with obesity or metabolic disease; the proposed mechanism in obesity involves adipose aromatase activity and higher oestrogen levels. An intact HPG axis is needed, so these agents cannot work in primary hypogonadism or secondary hypogonadism caused by organic HPG-axis damage. SERMs act as tissue-dependent ER agonists or antagonists, while AI prevent aromatase-mediated androgen conversion. Published evidence is poor and every such use is off-label. SERMs could predispose to venous thromboembolism through vascular agonist effects; patients should be warned about this possible risk although supporting data are lacking. Prolonged use can reduce bone density and cause osteoporosis, potentially raising fracture risk.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2.7 Gonadotropins
document_sections.content: Gonadotropin therapy should be considered standard for men with secondary hypogonadism who seek paternity. Recombinant hCG and LH have effects comparable to urine-derived preparations. A meta-analysis favours giving hCG together with FSH for better outcomes. Recombinant FSH also has effects comparable to urine-derived FSH.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for choice of treatment for LOH
document_sections.content: The evidence summary associates diet- and exercise-related weight loss with a small testosterone increase (LE 1a), identifies testosterone gels and long-acting injectable TU as having optimal safety profiles (LE 1a), and supports gonadotropins for fertility restoration in secondary hypogonadism (LE 1a). Strong recommendations are to treat organic causes when indicated; improve lifestyle, reduce weight, withdraw interfering drugs where possible, and treat comorbidities before testosterone therapy; and explain expected benefits and adverse effects while choosing a preparation jointly with the informed patient. A Weak recommendation favours starting high-risk men on testosterone gels rather than a long-acting depot.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.1 Hypogonadism and fertility issues
document_sections.content: Drug treatment aims to normalise testosterone and improve or resolve symptoms. Although exogenous testosterone is usually the first option for symptom treatment, it suppresses pituitary gonadotropins and impairs spermatogenesis and sperm maturation. Consequently, it is contraindicated in hypogonadal men seeking fertility treatment. With secondary hypogonadism, gonadotropin therapy may preserve normal testosterone and restore sperm production.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.2 Male breast cancer
document_sections.content: Studies indicate that testosterone and/or its conversion to E2 significantly influences male breast-cancer growth through several pathways. SERMs remain a therapeutic option for this cancer. Because evidence on testosterone therapy after successful breast-cancer treatment is unavailable, both treated and active male breast cancer are regarded as absolute contraindications.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.3 Lower urinary tract symptoms/benign prostatic hyperplasia
document_sections.content: In a six-month trial of 60 treated patients, residual urine and prostate volume did not change significantly; IPSS storage symptoms improved significantly despite increased PSA, and larger pretreatment prostate volume predicted LUTS improvement. In a placebo-controlled RCT of 120 hypogonadal men with total testosterone < 12 nmol/L, MetS, and planned BPH surgery, testosterone did not alter LUTS severity versus placebo but improved ultrasound inflammation markers and expression of several pro-inflammatory genes. Among 428 men followed on therapy for eight years, IPSS improved significantly, Qmax and residual urine did not change, and prostate volume increased significantly. RHYME followed 999 patients for three years and found no significant PSA or total-IPSS difference between treated and untreated men; the SIAMO-NOI registry of 432 men from fifteen centres reported similar findings. Meta-analyses likewise found no significant LUTS change versus placebo. Current literature gives no reason to discourage testosterone in hypogonadal men with BPH/LUTS and suggests limited benefit. Caution remains for severe LUTS at IPSS > 19 because exclusion from RCTs limits long-term safety evidence.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.4 Prostate cancer (PCa)
document_sections.content: Observational studies have not established an association between higher circulating testosterone and PCa. Studies of very low fT report reduced low-to-intermediate-grade PCa risk but a non-significantly higher chance of high-grade disease; the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, PCPT, and REDUCE described a similar pattern with differing significance. A meta-analysis of 27 placebo-controlled RCTs found no evidence of higher PSA after one year of therapy; its analysis of 11 studies found no evidence of increased PCa occurrence. One year may be too short for firm risk conclusions, although an analysis restricted to studies with > 1-year follow-up also found no significant PSA or PCa-risk increase. Across three registries involving > 1,000 treated patients with five years’ median follow-up, PCa occurrence remained below reported general-population incidence. An observational study of 10,311 treated men and 28,029 controls, median follow-up 5.3 years, reported similar findings and a lower PCa risk in the highest cumulative-dose tertile than in controls. TRAVERSE found no between-arm difference in overall or high-grade PCa during mean follow-up of 33.0 ± (SD) 12.1 months, but total PSA increased significantly more from baseline with testosterone than placebo. For PCa survivors, recurrence and progression safety is unestablished. Many case series have short follow-up, small samples, no controls, or heterogeneous patients and regimens. A meta-analysis of thirteen studies involving 608 patients, including 109 with prior high-risk PCa and follow-up of 1-189.3 months, suggested no increase in biochemical recurrence, but poor evidence limits interpretation. Another meta-analysis of 21 studies has similar limitations; both have high heterogeneity and few subjects. An RCT after prostatectomy for non-aggressive PCa is ongoing. Available literature does not support increased PCa risk during testosterone therapy, but testosterone must be avoided in advanced PCa. Because long-term prospective safety evidence for survivors is insufficient, treatment decisions require caution, full discussion of unknown long-term effects, and restriction to symptomatic, low-risk individuals.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.5 Cardiovascular Disease
document_sections.content: Hypogonadism is associated with increased CVD risk, but whether LOH causes atherosclerosis or follows from it is unresolved. LOH accompanies central obesity, insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia, pro-thrombotic tendency, and chronic inflammation; inflammatory cytokines from atherosclerosis can suppress HPG-axis testosterone release. RCTs in MetS or T2DM suggest improvements in several cardiovascular risk factors, but equivocal findings do not justify testosterone therapy outside treatment of specific symptoms. Studies associate LOH with greater all-cause and CVD-related mortality, and meta-analyses identify cardiovascular morbidity and mortality risk. Among men with angiographically documented coronary disease, low testosterone was associated with twice the risk of earlier death versus eugonadal men. Population studies found fewer cardiovascular events in the upper normal testosterone quartile than in the lower three quartiles. PCa androgen deprivation is linked to greater CVD and sudden-death risk, whereas two epidemiological studies associated high-normal testosterone with fewer cardiovascular events. ED can independently signal CVD and may be the first manifestation of atherosclerosis. Men with hypogonadism and/or ED should undergo individual cardiovascular-risk assessment. Risk factors should be assessed and treated in men with existing CVD or receiving androgen deprivation; clinicians prescribing testosterone should counsel patients, with cardiology referral when appropriate. No RCT definitively resolves testosterone's cardiovascular effects. The one-year TTrial (n=790), TIMES2 (n=220), BLAST, and frailty studies, and the T4DM 2-year study, did not find increased MACE. RCTs lasting three to twelve months in known cardiac disease found no MACE increase and reported better ischaemia, angina, and exercise capacity. A cohort study of n=20,4857 men, mean follow up 4.3 years, found no increased composite cardiovascular outcome with transdermal or intramuscular testosterone regardless of prevalent CVD. The EMA reported no consistent evidence of increased heart-problem risk, while requiring updated safety information and confirmation of deficiency through symptoms, signs, and laboratory tests before treatment. In the double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority TRAVERSE trial, testosterone was noninferior to placebo for MACE, although atrial fibrillation, acute kidney injury, and pulmonary embolism were mildly more frequent with testosterone; these observations require confirmation. Median follow-up of 5.1 years since the last injection in T4DM found no difference in self-reported new CVD diagnoses. Interventional evidence suggests no increased risk up to three years and neutral or beneficial MACE findings when testosterone normalises, but studies cannot exclude later or long-term cardiovascular events.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.5.1 Cardiac Failure
document_sections.content: Testosterone therapy is contraindicated in severe chronic cardiac failure because fluid retention may worsen it. Some studies suggest low doses achieving mid-normal testosterone may benefit moderate chronic cardiac failure. Untreated hypogonadism has been observed alongside higher readmission and mortality in heart failure. If chronic-cardiac-failure patients are treated, careful clinical follow-up and regular testosterone and haematocrit measurements are essential.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.6 Erythrocytosis
document_sections.content: Raised haematocrit is testosterone therapy's most common adverse effect and reflects stimulation of erythropoiesis. An increase above normal usually appears between three and twelve months after starting treatment; it can also follow dose escalation, a switch from topical to parenteral therapy, or development of a relevant respiratory or haematological comorbidity. There is no evidence of harm from a haematocrit increase up to and including 54%. Above 54%, studies associate haematocrit weakly with greater cardiovascular events and mortality independently of testosterone; those studies include varied causes of secondary polycythaemia, and none isolates testosterone-induced erythrocytosis. In TRAVERSE, pulmonary embolism occurred in 0.9% of the testosterone group versus 0.5% of the placebo group among symptomatic hypogonadal men aged 45-80 years with established or high CVD risk. Three earlier large studies found no evidence of increased venous-thromboembolism risk overall, although one observed a risk peak at six months after treatment initiation that subsequently declined. In another study, venous thromboembolism occurred in 42 cases, 40 of whom had underlying thrombophilia. A meta-analysis linked many events to previously unrecognised thrombophilia-hypofibrinolysis; another meta-analysis and systematic review found no increased venous-thromboembolism risk. An RCT in stable angina found no adverse change in measured coagulation markers. Higher baseline haematocrit, smoking, and respiratory disease increase the likelihood of elevated haematocrit during therapy. Parenteral products raise haematocrit more often than topical ones; a retrospective registry found more haematocrit results > 50% with long-acting testosterone undecanoate than with gels. Existing CVD calls for particular diagnostic certainty and haematocrit and testosterone monitoring. Without comorbidity or acute cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease, elevated haematocrit may be managed by reducing dose, changing formulation, or, if very high, venesection (500 mL), repeated if necessary, usually without stopping testosterone.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.7 Obstructive Sleep Apnoea
document_sections.content: Evidence does not show that testosterone therapy initiates or worsens sleep apnoea. CPAP combined with testosterone gel was more effective for obstructive sleep apnoea than CPAP alone. One RCT in severe sleep apnoea reported lower oxygen-saturation index and nocturnal hypoxaemia after seven weeks versus placebo; that difference was absent after eighteen weeks and was unrelated to baseline testosterone.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.8 Follow-up
document_sections.content: Testosterone therapy's symptomatic benefits develop over time; TTrials observed improved sexual symptoms as early as three months. Schedule the first review after three months, with another at six months or twelve months according to patient characteristics and biochemical results. Patients at high risk of raised haematocrit should be reviewed every three months during the first year and at least every six months thereafter. Guidance for polycythaemia vera advises maintaining haematocrit below 45%. In a multi-institutional cohort of treated hypogonadal men with total testosterone < 12 nmol/L, those developing polycythaemia at haematocrit > 52% (n=5,887), compared with those who did not (n=4,2784), had greater MACE or venous-thromboembolism risk, mainly in the first treatment year. Risk was higher at a 54% threshold; no risk was observed at 50%. TTrials targeted young-men's normal testosterone range of 280–873 ng/dL or 9.6-30 nmol/L and achieved a favourable benefit–risk balance; a similar follow-up target may be considered. Testosterone sampling time depends on formulation. Check PSA and haematocrit before and during treatment. Discuss PSA/DRE screening with men aged < 40 or > 70 years because PCa risk is low in the younger group and population-monitoring justification is insufficient in the older group. Baseline and at least annual glyco-metabolic assessment may be reasonable, especially for functional hypogonadism. Consider baseline and 18-24 months DEXA, particularly with more severe deficiency. DRE is mandatory at baseline and recommended at least annually during treatment, provided PSA velocity has not increased significantly. Follow local PCa guidance when deciding whether PSA rise or prostate findings warrant biopsy or stopping treatment. Broad consensus calls for withdrawal and phlebotomy if haematocrit rises > 54%, particularly in high-risk men; lower-risk patients may instead have dose reduction, formulation change, and venesection. Investigate and counsel patients with a family history of venous thromboembolism, and exercise caution with existing or elevated CVD risk.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations on safety and monitoring in testosterone treatment
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that testosterone is contraindicated when men with secondary hypogonadism seek fertility (LE 1a) and in active PCa or breast cancer, whose patients are generally excluded from RCTs (LE 1a). It reports no increased PCa risk but calls for long-term prospective validation (LE 1a); identifies limited evidence in severe LUTS because such patients are generally excluded from RCTs (LE 1a); finds no substantive evidence of increased MACE when testosterone is restored to normal (LE 1a); and finds no evidence of a relationship with mild, moderate, or CPAP-treated severe sleep apnoea (LE 1b). Weak recommendations are to counsel previously surgically treated, currently disease-free patients with localised PCa about insufficient long-term safety evidence; restrict treatment to low-recurrence-risk PCa patients after at least one year follow-up with PSA < 0.01 ng/mL; and cautiously treat patients with existing CVD, venous thromboembolism, or chronic cardiac failure when testosterone is required, with close assessment and regular testosterone and haematocrit testing, keeping haematocrit from exceeding 54%. Strong recommendations are to explain that safety after treated male breast cancer is unknown; assess cardiovascular risk before treatment; assess cardiovascular symptoms and monitor closely in established CVD; exclude a family history of venous thromboembolism before treatment; measure testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months and annually thereafter; adjust or stop therapy and perform venesection when necessary at haematocrit > 54%, then restart at a lower dose after normalisation and consider a topical formulation; evaluate polycythaemia vera or elevated-haematocrit-risk patients every three months in the first year and at least every six months subsequently; and measure total PSA in PCa survivors at three, six and twelve months in the first year and annually thereafter.
